#909. Which game will Chelsea's Palmer miss after red card?

Cole Palmer was sent off in the second half of Chelsea's 2-0 loss at Stamford Bridge

Chelsea's Cole Palmer will not miss the Blues' Premier League meeting with Manchester United on Saturday, despite being sent off in his side's last Premier League match.

Palmer was shown two yellow cards in the second half of the Blues' defeat by rivals Tottenham Hotspur on Saturday. That dismissal meant that Palmer was handed a one-match ban.

The England playmaker was shown his first caution for an off-the-ball incident involving Spurs' Mateus Fernandes. He was then shown a second yellow card for a foul on Conor Gallagher.

In most cases, this would be served in that team's next Premier League match. However, Palmer will not miss Chelsea's meeting with United at Stamford Bridge.

Instead, Palmer will be banned for the Blues' EFL Cup fourth-round match away at Liverpool on Wednesday night.

This is because red card suspensions are carried out across domestic competitions rather than being specific to the competition they were received in.

Suspensions for an accumulation of yellow cards across a campaign are served in the competition in which they are received.

So while the Blues will miss Palmer for their trip to Anfield, he will be available to face United three days after the club's cup tie on Merseyside.

#908. Familiarity of Doha drives home just how far Socceroos have come in recent years | Joey Lynch

There is increasing evidence of an evolution not only in approach but also mentality, highlighted by a return to the scene of Asian Cup heartbreak

Last week’s 3-0 dismissal of Qatar at the Abdullah bin Khalifa Stadium marked the first time the Socceroos had returned to the Gulf state since their heartbreaking elimination from the Asian Cup just under three years ago. Back then, coach Graham Arnold called Doha a “home away from home” after they relocated there during the Covid pandemic, and went so far as to suggest that they would have some form of advantage at the 2022 World Cup as a result.

Wandering around the city in 2026, memories rush back of Socceroos fans becoming eager participants in the takeover of the city’s souks during the World Cup. So too the feelings of sadness to see the birds still cooped up in small cages at the nearby bird market. It evokes recollections of trips on the red Metro line out to the Al Janoub Stadium in Al Wakrah, aided by the faded posters and stickers celebrating the 2022 tournament’s arrival that to this day can still be seen in shopfronts. There’s the excitement, for some, when a stray cat reminds you just how personable the local felines can be, as well as the sense of unease that remains whenever one pauses to reflect on how all this was built and the hands that did so.

But for all the familiarity and continuity for the Socceroos – five players who were there when Son Heung-min broke Australian hearts featured in Friday’s win – being back in Doha rams home just how much has changed for this team, and how well and truly into a new era we are.

Tony Popovic occupies the dugout these days, after the defeat to Korea arguably represented the beginning of the end of Arnold’s tenure by sparking a fatigue that would culminate in a downturn in results and his resignation later that year.

Nestory Irankunda, the rapidly emerging star of Popovic’s team who now has eight international goals to his name, was about to suffer a 4-0 defeat against the Central Coast Mariners nearly three years ago. Alessandro Circati was left out of the Socceroos squad to ensure he retained his place in the Parma side seeking to secure promotion to Serie A. Paul Okon-Engstler, Patrick Beach and Lucas Herrington were all yet to play senior football.

These players, who all started against Qatar, are emerging cornerstones of a new Socceroos setup that fielded the World Cup’s youngest side in North America, before flashing signs of further growth against Brazil in September. On Friday, this talented group bullied the two-time defending Asian champions on their own turf in the first-half, putting the game to bed before Popovic swung the changes and things got disjointed after half-time.

There is increasing evidence of an evolution not only in approach but also mentality. Of players bringing to the national team the lessons they’ve learned not just in the green and gold, but also in their experiences at bigger, more demanding clubs and leagues – in part because of the platform they’ve been offered by Popovic.

All of which could make it serendipitous if Tuesday’s game against Jordan, at the symbolic home of his predecessor, proves to be the end of the Popovic era.

Sign up for expert analysis from Jonathan Wilson as well as a rundown of Australians playing in the major leagues

The players aren’t going anywhere but with his contract situation still up in the air, it could well prove to be Popovic’s last game in charge of the Socceroos if he doesn’t agree to an extension. Given the postponement of January’s Asian Cup, there may not be the send-off he might have envisioned. Instead, a 12,000-seat stadium – unlikely to be very full – will host a hastily relocated friendly that’s entire raison d’être has vanished.

Remarkably, after sensitive discussions to relocate Tuesday’s game after player resistance to travelling to Amman, in line with DFAT advice, Doha could once again be pressed into action to serve as a historic backdrop for the Socceroos, just as a pandemic already saw it become the site of many a moment of distinction.

#907. Which Premier League players are set for yellow card suspensions?

Harry Maguire and Alexis Mac Allister are among 13 players on the brink of a one-match ban

The first one-match suspensions for yellow card offences in the 2026-27 Premier League season have now been served.

Hull City's Matt Crooks and Aston Villa's Matty Cash became the first players to receive a ban for accumulating five yellow cards before gameweek 19.

Players receive a one-match suspension if they pick up five or more yellow cards prior to the conclusion of their team's 19th league match of the season.

There are now 13 players sitting on four bookings after 10 rounds of matches, meaning they must avoid another yellow card prior to the halfway point of the season to avoid a ban.

Bournemouth have the most players on the brink of a ban, with three players one yellow card away from suspension.

After that date, the threshold increases to 10 yellow cards. Any player reaching that number before the end of their club's 32nd league match of the season will receive a two-match suspension.

From that point, there are further thresholds at 15 and 20 yellow cards.

For players reaching 15 cautions, they incur a three-match suspension. Punishments for players reaching 20 yellow cards are determined by a regulatory commission.

Those cut-offs do not reset until the end of the Premier League season.

In the Championship, League One and League Two, there are similar thresholds.

However, with those three divisions having 46 rounds of league matches instead of 38, players have to avoid getting 10 yellow cards before the end of the 37th league match in order to not receive a two-match suspension.

In those divisions, the yellow cards are reset at the end of the league season and do not include matches in the play-offs.

The following players have served a one-match ban and will now receive a two-match ban if they reach ten bookings before game week 32:

Matt Crooks - Hull City (five yellow cards)

If any of the following players receive another Premier League yellow card before the season's halfway point, they will be banned for one match:

Pascal Gross - Brighton & Hove Albion (four)

Oliver Boscagli - Brighton & Hove Albion (four)

The following players will miss their club's next set of fixtures:

Max Dowman - Arsenal (red card suspension)

Jean-Philippe Mateta - Crystal Palace (red card suspension)

Igor Thiago - Brentford (red card suspension)

#906. Fact check: Online disinformation rife after Krakow mass shooting

Fake and AI-manipulated images spread online in the hours after the Krakow attack, fueling false narratives about the mass shooting. DW Fact Check examined what's real, and what isn't.

A gunman killed six people in a shooting spree in Krakow's Old Town on Saturday, before being shot and detained by police. The gunman, who is also suspected of killing three family members before the attack, later died in hospital.

On Monday, Poland's national prosecutor's office announced a formal investigation.

Nevertheless, much is still unknown about the details of the crime, leaving social media users to fill the information vacuum with fake images of the attacker and alleged screenshots of his online profile. DW Fact Check breaks down the developing story.

Claim: A viral picture has been circulating on social media claiming to be the real image of the suspected attacker.

In the post, the image is posted with the caption, "[…] The perpetrator of the attack in Krakow is a 25-year-old Polish citizen, Polish police have reported. The death toll has reached six. (…)".

But the unusual sharpness of this picture raises doubt of its authenticity. It is difficult to imagine capturing such a clear image in a chaotic situation.

DW checked the image using two different AI detectors. Hive Moderation identified it as 99.5% AI-generated, while Google's SynthID Detector confirmed that it contains a SynthID watermark, indicating that it was generated or edited using Google's AI technology.

In our research we found several versions of the suspect image circulating online, most looking very similar. We also found a number of images and videos showing the attack.

Although DW cannot independently verify the footage, it shares similarities in terms of the people and background with some original images published by picture agencies.

It appears the AI-generated images may have been created using this footage as a reference. Some of the posts sharing these images have also been labeled as AI-generated.

One important thing to understand is that AI cannot sharpen a blurry image with correct details or recover details that are not visible in an original photograph. It can generate plausible details based on the surrounding visual information, but these are essentially guesses, not exact reproductions of what was actually there.

More about this and how users used sharpening AI tools here.

Claim: "Michal Oksinski, the terrorist from Krakow who also killed his parents and sister, had a Telegram account with the Ukrainian flag. On November 3, he wrote 'Thanks, Dad, for the gun', posting this photo of himself wearing the Ukrainian flag insignia," an X user wrote in a post viewed more than 700,000 times.

This Telegram channel is almost certainly inauthentic. The account allegedly posted a photo on November 3, showing the attacker holding a gun, standing in front of a television and a Ukrainian insignia on the wall.

Another post on November 4 simply reads, "11/7/2026", the date of the attack. Both of these posts were edited on November 8, after the suspect had been apprehended.

DW verified on the Telegram app by hovering over the posts to show the edit history. The channel's photo, a Ukrainian flag, was also edited after the attack took place.

This is a common disinformation tactic — fake accounts will edit old posts and pictures in the days after a breaking news event to give the appearance that they've predicted or announced the event in advance.

Further proof: in Poland, the date is written first, not the month. And the photo of the alleged attacker itself is almost certainly AI-generated. HIVE Moderation said it was 99.9% likely to be created with AI.

Claim: "#BREAKING: The attacker in Poland had a full arsenal in this trunk! He also has forward observation group patches, an American military company active in Ukraine," reads an X post viewed nearly 100,000 times. The attached photo of the supposed "arsenal" in the trunk has been shared by several other accounts.

The attached photo claims to show the attacker's car with a trunk full of guns, ammunition, a helmet and a military vest.

The vest in the trunk of the car features a symbol supposedly connected to the Forward Observations Group, an American tactical training lifestyle brand that has traveled to and operated in Ukraine.

The patch, however, is the Old Roger flag, a symbol commonly used in military circles. The Forward Observations Group logo is a variation of this symbol, featuring a horned skeleton holding a gun, not an hourglass.

This is also not the attacker's car from the scene of the crime. This license plate is registered with the Krakow police, indicating they likely collected evidence from the crime scene and moved it to this car.

Little details like these can help separate fact from fiction, especially in a rapidly evolving story like the Krakow shooting.

Daniel Ebertz contributed to this article.

#905. Man Utd expected to back Poch in January transfer window

Watch our 'Unfinished Business' Transfer Show special on Sky Sports News at 4pm and 7pm as we look ahead to January; Man Utd are expected to be active in the market with left-back, centre-back and a forward on the agenda for new head coach Mauricio Pochettino

Sky Sports News Reporter @DanyalHKhan

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Manchester United head coach Mauricio Pochettino is expected to be backed in the January transfer window as the club aim to address their disappointing start to the season.

A left-back, centre-back and forward are areas the club are looking to potentially strengthen in January with Pochettino expected to have input on targets they will pursue.

Despite the club's hierarchy feeling the team should be further up the table, there is also an acknowledgement that they could have further strengthened the squad in the summer in areas where they lacked depth.

Sky Sports News understands Manchester United already had plans to move in the upcoming window under former head coach Michael Carrick, before he was sacked last month following United's worst start to a league season for 40 years.

However, Pochettino is now expected to be consulted in the coming weeks and will have his say on potential recruits in January.

Tune in to Sky Sports News at 4pm and 7pm for our 'Unfinished Business' Transfer Show special for in-depth analysis of Man Utd's plans for the January window.

Fulham's Calvin Bassey and Everton's Jarrad Branthwaite are two players United are monitoring as potential options to reinforce their defence in January.

Despite Fulham's struggles this season, Bassey is a player who has impressed and has just six months left on his current deal, though his club have the option to extend that by a further year.

Fulham head coach Alvaro Arbeloa has described the 26-year-old as one of the best defenders in the world and said the club's aim is to extend Bassey's contract.

Meanwhile, Branthwaite has long been admired by United. In 2024, United had two bids rejected for the centre-back, their second being worth around £50m.

Everton are in a strong negotiating position over the 24-year-old, who has a contract until the summer of 2030.

United are looking at left-footed centre-back options as they consider potential replacements for Lisandro Martinez. His future at Old Trafford looks in doubt come next summer with his current contract expiring.

Despite United having an option for a further 12 months, he is unlikely to be offered fresh terms as Sky Sports News reported last month.

The club decided not to pursue a left-back in the summer as they focused on their midfield rebuild with the belief their long-term targets would be more attainable next year.

It remains to be seen whether that will be true come the end of the season and where that leaves players such as Newcastle United's Lewis Hall, but with five different players being used in that position with limited success, the club will look at the possibility of cover at left-back in January.

Fulham left-back Antonee Robinson continues to be monitored, as first reported by Sky Sports News in March. Fulham are aware of widespread interest in Robinson but no club has so far made a move for the 29-year-old, who worked under Pochettino with the USA.

Barcelona's Alejandro Balde was a player linked with United in the summer but was never at a stage when the move seemed likely. United were aware of his potential availability and it has not been ruled out that they revisit a deal in January if it works for all parties.

Manchester City's Rayan Ait-Nouri was an option United tentatively explore on Deadline Day but they decided against pursuing him due to City's insistence on an obligation to make the move permanent. Sky Sports News understands he is not considered a target at this stage as United look at other options.

With United's main No 9 Benjamin Sesko ruled out until at least January, the club will explore potential reinforcements in the upcoming window to re-balance the club's attack.

Although United scored seven goals in their last two games before the break, the club have missed a physical presence in Sesko's absence to lead the line.

Leeds United's Dominic Calvert-Lewin was a player of interest but his future looks likely to remain at Elland Road and United are not expected to explore a move for the forward.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Any outgoings in January could have an impact on how much the club can reinforce Pochettino's squad but numerous first-team departures are not likely with the size of the squad and long-term injuries as well as Pochettino needing time to assess his squad all set to play a factor.

Joshua Zirkzee continues to be a player who attracts interest from Italy and United could entertain a move for the Dutch forward if they receive a suitable offer but would need cover in that position.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Martinez's future will under the spotlight in January. Sky Sports News reported last month United are unlikely to offer him a new contract. His current deal expires next summer although the club hold an option for a further 12 months.

Pochettino will also have to manage other expiring contracts in his squad with Harry Maguire, Luke Shaw and captain Bruno Fernandes also in the last six months of their current contracts, although it is worth noting the club have a 12-month option on Fernandes and Maguire.

#903. A long wait, some magic and that smile: Ronaldinho savours Ravenna debut at 46

Brazilian legend, an investor at Serie C club, showed glimpses of old brilliance as he played 45 minutes for the promotion-chasing side

It may have been the longest buildup in world football. In June, the former Barcelona and Brazil legend Ronaldinho was unveiled by the Serie C side Ravenna to make his comeback at the age of 46 – 11 years after his last official game. Then silence.

But on a chilly November day on the eastern coast of Italy, there he was, not only in the squad, but in the starting XI for the eagerly anticipated derby against Forlì as Ravenna chase promotion.

The Ravenna manager, Andrea Mandorlini, deployed Ronaldinho in a central position, just behind the striker Simone Rabbi. The Brazilian held his position well, but was slow to get going. As the game progressed, he warmed up and showed his excellent skills; some things do not appear to change. Ronaldinho touched the ball 25 times, took three corners – one of which nearly led to a Ravenna goal – and initiated the move that led to the hosts taking the lead in the 35th minute.

Having trained with the team just once, whether he plays again remains to be seen. But he had already sprinkled some magic on a club and a region that has not made headlines in years. He played the first half as Ravenna won 2-0 to stay second in the division’s Group B (the Italian third tier is divided into three regional sections). Only the group winners earn promotion and Ravenna trail Spezia by six points.

Whatever happens for the remainder of the season this has put the club back on the football map. Ravenna’s highest finish was eighth in Serie B, in 1996-97, but this match was broadcast live by Sky Sports in Italy and shown in several other countries. It even appeared on the giant screens in New York’s Times Square, where the club’s owners, the Cipriani family, have built much of their international reputation through Harry’s Bar.

The town’s mayor, Alessandro Barattoni, who, as always, was watching the game from the stands, said: “A champion like Ronaldinho, a world football icon, brings great visibility and today is an opportunity for us to showcase Ravenna around the world, from our stadium. It is something new for us and together with the club the municipality will try to understand how this can have a positive impact on the town.”

The local community had been excited at the prospect of Ronaldinho representing the club, but there was some regret, too. “It would have been nice if he had come to take a stroll around the city, among the people who live here and own the shops,” the barista Barbara said before the game.

So how did he end up here? The Brazilian is a friend of Ignazio Cipriani, the owner of the Giallorossi. Lorenzo Tonetti and Ariedo Braida, old acquaintances from Ronaldinho’s time at Milan, are also part of the club. They convinced him to become an investor in the club and to pull on his boots again. In addition, Ravenna are now wearing his R10 sportswear line and one of the stands bears the same name.

Ravenna are aiming high. Cipriani has never hidden the fact he is aiming for Serie A, which is ambitious for a city with a population of 156,000. And Sunday brought hope, Dinho stepping on to the pitch in a gold-trimmed kit picked by the club to celebrate his arrival (and available for sale at €120). His hair was kept in check by a black headband and he was wearing gloves on a chilly afternoon. On his back, the No 10, something more than just a number for him, the man who became a global hero thanks to his extraordinary skill and contagious smile.

A younger generation has been able to discover Ronaldinho’s genius through the endless supply of online videos showcasing his greatest moments. Children who have never seen him play know his tricks and signature moves, while their parents can relive an era of football they may feel no longer exists.

“Dad, was he strong?” a young girl asked her father as they walked hand in hand towards the stadium. “Yes, he was strong. Actually, he is strong,” he corrected himself.

Our picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown in

One family had left Rome at 5am and travelled the 350km north just because their son had watched Ronaldinho on YouTube and wanted to see him live. Others had travelled even further, with supporters arriving from Turkey and Canada.

Ronaldinho hahas scored 299 professional goals, but his landmark 300th on his return was not to be. However, in front of a record attendance of 6,743 the way he initiated the move for Giulio Donati’s goal was ample reward for those who had turned up. Donati made his Serie A debut on 29 August 2010 for Lecce, at San Siro, against Milan, marking the Brazilian that day.

As Ronaldinho walked off at half-time, he was surrounded by a media scrum. After the game, he spoke of his desire to play again. “It all went by too quickly,” he said. “Football is like that, it’s always been like that for me.”

Who knows, perhaps he enjoyed himself so much that he wants to extend his career even further. “I don’t know, but if the president calls me, I’ll come back. It’s always a pleasure to play, I told him: ‘when he needs me, I’m there’.”

Mandorlini was effusive too. “We’re here and we’re truly proud to have been the architects of this match you played in,” he told the Brazilian. “So, if you want to play another one, that’s fine.”

Who knows what the future holds? For now, Ravenna fans will always have this: a day when a true legend connected people from around the world and allowed them, for one afternoon, to dream.

#901. Azeez to Andrés: seven smart-looking Premier League deadline day deals

An 18-year-old who has played at two major international tournaments and the division’s top clearance maker from last season also feature

A tricky, exciting, quick and versatile midfielder, Azeez has proven himself in the Championship with Millwall over the past two seasons and now deserves a chance to test himself in the top flight.

Brighton had been chasing him for a while and struck a deal on deadline day for a very reasonable reported initial £12.5m, rising to £15m. If he can make the step up and produce anything like his second-tier form, he’ll be a steal.

He is a high-volume producer at the sharp end of the pitch, constantly making things happen that threaten the opposition’s goal, but standing out most for his crossing. He ranked top of the Championship last season for open-play crosses (227) and expected assists from crosses (6.71 xA).

He also ranked fourth for dribble attempts (131), ninth for shots (95), sixth for chances created from open play (58). He created good-quality chances, too; only two players created more big chances than he did (18), and he ranked fourth for expected assists. His 9.12 xA alongside only seven assists suggests he may benefit from playing alongside better finishers.

A hugely exciting prospect. Despite being 18, Mbaye has significant and noteworthy experience under his belt. Last year he made six appearances, including in the final, for Senegal at the Africa Cup of Nations and this summer he made four appearances at the World Cup. He has also played in two Ligue 1 title-winning campaigns, including 2024-25, when he became the youngest player in PSG’s history to start a game, and won the Champions League in both of those seasons

He is a dribbling and ball-carrying menace, who always looks as if he’s about to do something special. Among players to play at least 900 minutes in Ligue 1 last season, he was 11th for carries (moving at least five metres with the ball) per 90, with 20.0, and 12th for progressive carries (moving at least five metres upfield with the ball) per 90, with 10.3. Most of the players above him in both lists are defenders, who naturally have more space to move into.

He was third for take-on-ending carries, or running with the ball for at least five metres before attempting to beat an opponent with a dribble, with 2.9 per 90. And he also has end product to boot. He scored at Afcon and the World Cup despite limited minutes and his 0.45 goals or assists per 90 for PSG last season is not to be sniffed at.

Danso had a pretty impossible task over his two years at Tottenham. He was the back-up to the first-choice centre-backs Cristian Romero and Micky van de Ven, playing intermittently on both sides of central defence in dysfunctional teams jumping between styles of play, and he very rarely played for any consistent run of games.

He was unfairly compared with the players he was replacing for much of his time there, but the truth is he was always reliable enough. He excelled, however, when Romero got injured during the run-in last season and he was called upon in Spurs’ time of need as they scraped clear of relegation.

He may not be the best on the ball – though he is hardly terrible – but he is an excellent deep defender. Among those to play at least 1,000 minutes in the Premier League last season, Danso ranked first for clearances (8.2 per 90) and headed clearances (6.3), and was fifth for aerial duels won (4.8 per 90).

He could thrive at Sunderland, who spent more of their out-of-possession game time in a low block than any other team in the Premier League last season (25%). Danso could be perfectly at home in this setup, paired alongside the player he beat into second place for clearances and headed clearances: Dan Ballard.

It was always said during Pep Guardiola’s time at Manchester City that attackers had their wings clipped in terms of individual freedom, limited to playing within the parameters of the manager’s meticulous gameplan.

But dribbling ability became increasingly important in the final years of his reign, with Jérémy Doku and Antoine Semenyo on the wings and Rayan Cherki in between. Doku (162) and Semenyo (144) ranked first and second for dribbles attempted in the Premier League last season, with Cherki ninth (111). They also ranked first (84), fourth (59) and eighth (51), respectively, for dribbles completed.

With the deadline-day addition of Ndiaye, City have gone in even harder on dribbling ability under Enzo Maresca. The Senegal international ranked second for dribbles attempted (136) and dribbles completed (73) in the Premier League last season.

Fernandez-Pardo’s versatility is a major attraction. He’s comfortable playing off the left and cutting in on to his right foot, or as a No 9. Although not the bulkiest, he has explosive pace and promises to be a threat in behind.

The Belgium international is arguably at his most threatening when running with the ball because he does so with such purpose. His 122 carries progressing the ball at least 10 metres upfield in Ligue 1 last term were bettered by only seven players, several of whom were defenders.

On top of that, he ranked top for carries into the penalty area (69) and seventh for carries ending with a shot or chance created (39).

Fofana appeared to be enjoying a swift rise in 2024-25, only for a serious ankle injury to massively disrupt his development in 2025-26. Sunderland will be hoping they can get him back to the levels shown the season before last, when he was a real livewire on Lyon’s left flank.

He contributed nine goal involvements (five goals, four assists) in 1,586 minutes in Ligue 1 in 2024-25, averaging one every 176 minutes. Only eight forwards (900+ mins) averaged more expected assists per 90 (0.25).

The most eye-catching aspects of his game, however, were his dynamism and pace. He could be difficult to stop once moving, and this made him a very useful outlet. Among Ligue 1 forwards (900+ mins), his 16.6 carries per 90 ranked him sixth, and he moved up to third for progressive carries per 90 (11.5).

Fofana is direct, exciting and has significant potential. He is a player Sunderland could make a profit on if he reaches the levels previously expected.

Andrés arrived to bolster Brighton’s midfield options after Carlos Baleba’s exit to Manchester United. Although a different type of midfielder to the Cameroonian, Chema is another with vast potential.

A product of Real Madrid’s academy, Chema joined Stuttgart last summer. During his sole campaign in the Bundesliga, he was in and out of the team but caught the eye at the base of their midfield.

Comparisons have been made to Rodri because of his physical attributes and nominal role as a holding midfielder. He doesn’t have anything like the same influence in possession but Chema is tidy on the ball.

It’s what he offers defensively that is most notable, however. He’s been broadly praised for his anticipation and reading of the game, ranking second among midfielders (900+ mins) since the start of last season for interceptions per 90 in the Bundesliga (2.3).

#900. Borussia Dortmund's Felix Nmecha and the question of religion

Felix Nmecha's "Crowns down" celebration has drawn criticism from a Borussia Dortmund fan club, reopening debate over faith, inclusion and religious messaging in football.

Felix Nmecha's renewed use of the "Crowns down celebration" — where a crown is pretended to be removed from someone's head and placed at Jesus' feet — has sparked a reaction from Borussia Dortmund's official supporters' group.

"Faith does not justify exclusion. Faith does not justify division. Borussia Dortmund is a club for everyone," read a statement after the Bundesliga club beat Elversberg, a game in which Nmecha scored twice. Nmecha's first documented "Crowns down celebration" was at the 2026 World Cup, for which "The King's Return" campaign was launched.

"In the past, the the Borussia Dortmund supporters club has deliberately refrained from commenting on sports-related issues and the athletic performance of individual players. We remain committed to this approach," the statement continued.

"However, when it comes to our club's values, discrimination, and the question of what view of humanity is fostered within and around Borussia Dortmund, we cannot and will not remain silent."

The fan club states their issue is not with Nmecha being a devout Christian, but rather his public support for "The King's Return" campaign, which the supporters club said "gives us cause to reassess the situation."

This campaign, according to research by German public broadcaster ARD in the summer of 2026, was designed by the "Ballers in God" (BIG) network. BIG was founded in 2015 by footballer John Bostock, a devout Christian who wanted to create a community where professional footballers could strengthen each other in their faith, pray together, and read the Bible. In over a decade since, the BIG community has grown to nearly 800,000 followers on Instagram.

Nmecha issued a response on social media not long afterwards, writing:

"I've been told that my most recent goal celebration has led to some misunderstandings," Nmecha wrote.

"My message was never intended to spread intolerance, discrimination, or hatred in any form. As Christians, our message is one of love and respect for every person—regardless of where someone comes from, what they believe in, or what worldview they hold."

Reports suggest that both the board at Dortmund and Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp will speak to Nmecha on the matter in the coming days.

The fan club say their criticism is "directed at religious networks that, under the guise of faith, promote a worldview in which people are devalued or marginalized because of their sexual orientation, gender identity, lifestyle, or personal choices... When religious beliefs are used to deny people their dignity or equality, that is where our tolerance for intolerance ends."

Here, they are referring to the recent ARD investigation. That work revealed the homepage for "The King's Return" campaign featured a link to a live counseling chat run by US-based evangelical nonprofit Groundwire. During the investigations, counselors told reporters that abortion is "Satan's plan" and that homosexuality is a sin.

Borussia Dortmund's statement of core values commits the club to diversity, human rights, and inclusion regardless of gender, sexual orientation, faith, or background. The club's largest and most influential fan group also promotes progressive, anti-fascist, and inclusive values. It is also part of a wider fan landscape in Germany where club members are more involved in club decisions than in many other countries. This was evidenced when the club signed a deal with arms manufacturer Rheinmetall two years ago and in the case of Nmecha as well. When the midfielder signed for Dortmund in 2023, many of the club's fans protested because the player had previously shared or liked several transphobic and homophobic posts on his Instagram account. In response, Nmecha deleted some posts and instead issued a statement emphasizing "I do not discriminate against anyone."

Article 4 of German Basic Law guarantees that each individual is allowed to decide how strongly, why and which god to believe in. In football, players cannot display political, religious, or personal slogans, statements, or images on their jerseys, undershirts, or gear. However, physical gestures are allowed so long as they don't delay the game or antagonize the crowd.

The use of physical religious gestures has history in sports, as professor Paul Putz described in his book "The Spirit of the Game: American Christianity and Big-Time Sports". Putz describes how the the pioneers of the Christian athlete movement realized they: "could influence others to Christian ideals more effectively on the field than in the pulpit."

And yet, such gestures can also be at odds with the atmosphere of modern sports arenas, particularly football. In their book "Sports and Christianity: Historical and Contemporary Perspectives", Nick J. Watson and Andrew Parker explain how modern sport has become a substitute for traditional faith.

"Sport seduces the teeming 'global village'; it is the new opiate of the masses; it is one of the great modern experiences … Sport, for many, has replaced religion as a source of emotional catharsis and spiritual passion," they wrote.

With the 26-year-old Nmecha a key player for both club and country, the conversation around faith and football looks set to continue for some time yet.

#899. Verhoeven to fight Wilder? 'He's always up for a big fight!'

Rico Verhoeven could potentially step in to fight Deontay Wilder on the undercard of Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff on December 11; Cruiserweight star Jai Opetaia was originally due to box Wilder in a heavyweight contest but had to withdraw

Sports Journalist @johndennen

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Deontay Wilder is now looking for a new opponent for his fight on the Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua undercard.

Wilder was due to box Jai Opetaia at the Principality Stadium on December 11, but Opetaia had to withdraw from their heavyweight bout and will stay at cruiserweight.

Wilder will remain on the card but the race is on to select a new opponent for him.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Rico Verhoeven could be a viable candidate. A kickboxing superstar, earlier this year the Dutchman went straight into a world title fight with legendary Ukrainian Oleksandr Usyk.

Verhoeven performed surprisingly well in that WBC championship fight in Giza. Although he was stopped in the 11th round, he had looked to threaten a monumental upset.

The Dutchman is now considering his next move and his team didn't rule out stepping in for Opetaia to fight Wilder in December.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"Plenty of interesting things happening right now," Verhoeven's manager Karim Erja told Sky Sports.

"We're exploring some exciting options for Rico, but you know him, he's always up for a big fight.

"Let's see what happens in the coming few days."

#898. From postcards to texts, the different ways a manager gets the sack - Pulis

When you hear about a manager parting company with a club, he has usually either been sacked or has resigned, but there are actually lots of different ways you can leave.

Over the years I spent working at every level of the game in England, from the bottom to the top, I have witnessed and been involved in many break-ups.

Some are smooth but others are far more fractious and don't happen face-to-face. I've witnessed managers being sacked over the phone or by text, or hearing they are losing their job by word of mouth.

One of the most soul-destroying times for a manager is when speculation is rife regarding not only your imminent sacking, but also about who is going to replace you.

During my career, I've known certain individuals who actually put their names forward for jobs before a manager is even sacked. Some go to the club involved through agents, some directly to the owners themselves.

Many managers are sounded out before eventually being appointed and another policy which has become popular with clubs is to drop names out to the press about possible replacements, to see the supporters' reactions to the names in the frame.

For the manager who is still in place, and whose stress levels are through the roof, it is devastating... but it is just another part of the job that you have to handle.

I've experienced that situation myself, in a scenario which went on for many months. Your confidence, not only in yourself but also in the club's hierarchy, takes another massive knock.

When it happened to me, I'd heard about the club's intentions from people in the media at quite an early stage and also worked out where the new manager would be coming from, but I had to bite my lip - myself and my staff were under contract, so we had to just carry on.

We kept pulling results out of the bag which delayed the inevitable, but eventually I knew my time was up.

Michael Carrick was sacked by Manchester United this week, but the club opened talks with Mauricio Pochettino before Carrick's departure was decided or confirmed

When they are getting treated this way, you can hardly blame managers for sometimes wanting to stick two fingers up to the people in charge.

One story comes to mind of a manager I know who was relieved of his duties by being placed on gardening leave while the club found a way to release him permanently.

During that time, and while he was still getting paid, the manager decided to go on holiday somewhere hot with his family. After watching his old team lose on TV in the sunshine, he sent a postcard to his chairman, which simply said 'wish you were here!'.

When he got home, he was sacked - but I bet he was still glad he did it!

Sadly, most managers don't get that kind of satisfaction - and often you don't even get a chance to say a proper goodbye to the players and staff you have worked closely with for many months or years.

My first spell at Stoke ended when I was driving up the motorway from my home in Bournemouth for the first day of pre-season in the summer of 2005.

I'd had a pretty good idea of what might happen since the end of the previous season but, over the next few weeks, the club's Icelandic owners did not say a word - until then.

I didn't have a problem with the decision, by the way. They were nice people and my view has always been 'if you don't want me, you don't want me'.

Anyway, I'd already been driving for four hours and, just as I got to the junction that would take me to the ground, my phone rang. It was the chairman, who told me he'd been meaning to call.

I was told I was no longer the manager, but also that I could not enter the stadium at any cost - I soon understood the urgency of the situation because it turned out the new manager had already arrived there. I had to just turn the car around, and head back home.

That kind of thing can happen to any manager, and you learn to be ready for it.

As a player, Burrows helped third-tier Swindon Town shock Arsenal in the 1969 League Cup final. As a manager, he had spells in charge of Portsmouth, Cardiff City (both twice) and Swansea and was also assistant manager at West Brom

I always remember playing at Swansea in one of my early games in my first job with Bournemouth, and their manager Frank Burrows inviting me into his office afterwards.

Frank, who sadly passed away in 2021, was a wonderful man and also a superb old-school manager who was always happy to offer advice to younger coaches and share his experiences.

We were having a drink and I noticed he had this big empty cardboard box next to his desk. I asked him what it was for, and he said it was to hold all his belongings - from his files on players to his family photographs - that were in his office.

"All the important stuff I'd like to keep is on the top of my desk," Frank said. "And every time I lose my job, because that time always comes, I can just sweep it into the box and off I go again. That box has travelled around the football world with me."

That always stuck with me. Management is such a precarious occupation that every manager has to think about that box, even if they don't have it sitting next to their desk every day!

It was not long afterwards that I found out what it was like to be sacked for the first time.

I still had a year left on my contract with Bournemouth but the chairmanship of the club changed and, in the summer of 1994, I was out.

It was hard enough to go from doing almost everything at the club to doing nothing, not even going in for pre-season training - but, because it was my hometown club, I also had to come to terms with listening to stories of my children being teased about my exit at school.

I also had my mortgage and my family to look after and unfortunately Bournemouth were not very helpful with the money they owed me.

It's a lot to think about, when you have just been thrown out into the real world, especially when it's a world you have no experience in or any other qualifications to fall back on. I was lucky enough to get another chance in management, but not every young manager does.

Fortunately, I've not always left clubs on bad terms, either. I've already mentioned a few difficult separations, but I've had some happier endings too.

Gibson appointed Pulis as Boro boss in December 2017. They reached the play-offs that season, then missed out on sixth place in the Championship by a single point in 2018-19

I've talked a lot in these columns about my affection for Peter Coates and his wonderful family. As well as owning Stoke City, they are a special group of people who have been unbelievably successful in their own ways, but they have never lost that human touch.

When the time came for me to part company with the club in 2013, they did so in a proper manner - Peter and John, his son and now chairman, were dead straight with me about wanting to go in a different direction, and made a difficult situation into a respectful parting of the ways.

I spent almost 10 years at Stoke over two spells but, while I was only at Middlesbrough for 18 months, it was a similar story with their owner and chairman Steve Gibson.

Steve has spent his entire life looking out for Boro but his commitment to his club goes far beyond being a lifetime supporter. He cares deeply for the people of that area and has devoted so much of his hard-earned cash towards making Boro a success.

I loved my time there because of the warmth of Steve and his family, and beyond. The area reminded me so much of south Wales, where the community was cherished and people, especially at the club, could not do enough for you.

After the last game of the 2018-19 season I was completely shot, and frustrated that we had not reached the Championship play-offs. My drive home that night was long and lonely but I felt worn out.

Once the dust had settled on that season, Steve and I met up in London. Our discussions were honest and open but my contract was up and we both agreed it was a good time for me to leave - I wanted it to end on good terms, and we certainly did that.

After dinner we had a fair few drinks and it ended up being a very, very late night. We arranged to have breakfast the following morning but I told him I have always been an early riser so, by 6am, I was up and on my way to the station to get back home.

My wife had just picked me up in Bournemouth at just after 8am when Steve rang to ask if I was down for breakfast yet - and he didn't believe me when I said no, I am back home.

I missed breakfast, but we remained good friends. Steve is a class act and I always hold Boro up as a club that deserves to be successful because of the attitude, commitment and honesty of everyone we came across.

My family still talk about how much they loved going there, and were genuinely disappointed when I left - something that doesn't apply to all my former clubs, obviously!

Tony Pulis was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

#897. Transfer window verdict: how every Premier League club fared

The British transfer record was equalled and one club signed no fewer than 18 players in another hectic summer

Bringing in Christos Tzolis, Bruno Guimarães and Ezri Konsa was a strong start to the window but could Arsenal’s failure to sign a marquee attacker cost them in the long run? They began targeting Morgan Rogers before pivoting to Vinícius Júnior when the England forward went to Chelsea, only to end up disappointed when Vinícius signed a new deal with Real Madrid. Julián Alvarez made clear he had no intention of joining from Atlético Madrid in the final days of the window and Arsenal kept their powder dry despite sanctioning the exits of Gabriel Jesus to Barcelona and Ethan Nwaneri to Borussia Dortmund. Should Gabriel Martinelli complete his move to Al-Hilal as expected in the coming days – the Saudi Pro League window remains open – a few injuries could leave Arteta short. Ed Aarons

Key ins: Bruno Guimarães (Newcastle, £75m), Ezri Konsa (Aston Villa, £51m), Piero Hincapié (Bayer Leverkusen, £45m), Christos Tzolis (Club Brugge, £34m)

Key outs: Leandro Trossard (Besiktas, £15.3m), Jakub Kiwior (Porto, £14.5m), Gabriel Jesus (Barcelona, £8.6m), Fábio Vieira (Hamburg, £7.7m), Christian Nørgaard (Everton, £7m), Ethan Nwaneri (Borussia Dortmund, loan)

It is all change at Villa and, although a little trepidation is inevitable, a refresh was probably overdue. At the same time, Unai Emery did not want to lose so many key players and Villa’s manager has made clear there is no such thing as a transition season in his eyes. Villa have generated about £300m from the sales of nine players and brought in 10 at a cost of about £250m. Villa have lowered their wage bill and changed the profile of their squad. Zion Suzuki, Ibrahim Mbaye and Johan Manzambi, names on the lips of Villa’s rivals, are particularly exciting signings. Last summer there was concern Villa had gone stale and 12 months ago they ended up fretting on deadline day – Harvey Elliott and Jadon Sancho joined on loan – but there was no such chaos this time. Ben Fisher

Perhaps Bournemouth’s best business was keeping hold of their coveted key players, chiefly Eli Junior Kroupi, Rayan, Alex Scott and Tyler Adams. Bournemouth rejected bids from Chelsea for Scott and stayed true to their plan of resisting offers to give Marco Rose the best chance of succeeding, with the club attempting to juggle European competition and the league for the first time. The arrival of the Portugal centre-back António Silva, 22, from Benfica looks a typically smart replacement for Marcos Senesi, 29. Kroupi’s freak foot injury, which will probably keep him out until November, may have proved a blessing in disguise in terms of retaining the 20-year-old. BF

#896. 60 minutes of perfection, 30 minutes of chaos - an England win for the ages

Harry Kane scored for a record-equalling seventh England away game

Thomas Tuchel went with bold words when reminded about the caution that sabotaged England's World Cup hopes and left them with so much to prove against Spain in the Nations League on Sunday.

In a media theatre at the Metropolitano in Madrid, head coach Tuchel's sixth sense led him to go public with what he was convinced England would produce against the world champions.

Tuchel looked his inquisitors in the eyes and declared: "We are up for something spectacular."

To say Tuchel and England kept their word was a masterpiece of understatement after the finest night of the head coach's reign resulted in a 3-2 victory that was large parts magnificent, some parts madness - and all parts spectacular.

It also ended Spain's 43-game unbeaten run - setting aside their penalty shootout defeat by Portugal in the 2025 Nations League final.

If England and Tuchel could be accused of being cowed by pressure when they led Argentina in the ill-fated World Cup semi-final, they were thrillingly positive in this unforgiving Madrid environment.

The question being asked when England held a one-goal advantage through Harry Kane's penalty at half-time was 'what would theirs and Tuchel's reaction be?' Stick or twist?

Would Tuchel tell England to press their foot on the pedal for acceleration? Or would he take the approach of going into reverse gear, as he did to ill-fated effect against Argentina?

How did England cling on against Spain and what did Tuchel do differently?

Who swaggered around like he owned the place? Spain v England ratings

England hold on to stun world champions Spain in thriller

The answer was delivered when they added goals from Arsenal duo Ezri Konsa and Ben White in the first 12 minutes of the second half.

This being England, they then created a mess for themselves when Elliot Anderson was sent off for fouling Lamine Yamal in the area after 65 minutes, although the main culprit was Jarell Quansah for initially conceding possession.

Mikel Oyarzabal scored from the spot and, when Yamal set up Nico Williams for Spain's second with 15 minutes left, it looked like more than an hour of faultless England football might be wasted.

But not a bit of it, as goalkeeper James Trafford produced heroics and England defended with every fibre to close out this landmark win.

Was this the statement victory that was almost demanded of Tuchel as recompense for the World Cup disappointment, a performance to convince the doubters?

"We're fully aware what we put out there," said Tuchel afterwards. "What a performance we put out for 65 minutes to be deservedly 3-0 up.

"Of course, the red card and the penalty changed the momentum and the characteristics of the game... but we know, and the players know very, very well, what they put out there. That is the statement - and that is the significance of this victory."

Simple details of the game barely touch the sides of a night filled with quality and glorious chaos, vindication for Tuchel and England's positive approach.

Spain opened with an ostentatious parade of the World Cup in front of England's players as the teams lined up, perhaps a psychological reminder of the superiority that has seen them dominate international football.

What followed, at times literally, reduced Spain's supporters to stunned silence and their players to a shell-shocked shambles chasing the shadows that were overpowering them.

England's white shirts were everywhere but Spain could not get near them. The tormentors had become the tormented.

It was alien territory for a Spain side that has carried all before them, while England's fans tucked away high in a corner of this vast arena were equally unbelieving as a dream unfolded in front of them.

England, for 65 minutes, were in a different class to Spain. And, yes, you have read that right.

From the first whistle, employing a suffocatingly high press, England ran all over Spain.

When White crowned a superb move with the third goal four minutes after Konsa's second, it looked, remarkably, to be a case of how big England's victory margin would be.

In the end, the margin was narrow but the stature and significance of England's victory was huge.

Tuchel labelled this meeting with Spain as "proof of concept at the highest level".

There was no doubt the German manager and England were under fierce scrutiny after the manner of the collapse, mentally and tactically, against Argentina at the World Cup.

Here they delivered the proof they can match the best then beat them.

Win over world champions Spain is a 'statement' - Tuchel

If the vital signs were being forensically examined for evidence Tuchel has learned lessons from a chastening World Cup, that England have improved after that harrowing experience, this game delivered these conclusions.

Of course, England must do it again. Do it when the pressure and expectation in at its highest.

The Nations League is competitive but cannot be compared to a World Cup and European Championship, both titles currently in the possession of the team they beat here.

But England's world-class players delivered - Kane inevitably with his 93rd international goal, but Jude Bellingham was on a level of his own, the outstanding performer on both sides with an individual display simply confirming he is the player with everything.

And Tuchel got his big calls right, especially selecting Trafford, who responded superbly in a frantic closing phase. White, making a strong claim for the right-back berth, not only scored a goal but produced crucial challenges in the face of relentless, albeit belated, Spain pressure.

"This was the highest level in terms of belief, team spirit, togetherness," said Tuchel. "It was on the highest level football wise in all aspects of the game. We did everything that needs to be done together.

"The deep build-up. The high press. The counter-attack. The tracking. The defensive phases. This was an excellent performance and of course a wonderful feeling for us in the dressing room.

"We overcame some difficult moments in the end. That's how it is. But we are very well aware which steps we took now through after the World Cup."

England's win means they top their Nations League group, but the importance spreads much wider than simply a league table.

The first 65 minutes were simply breathtaking. Spain wilting under attack after attack. Spain rattled until they shook as England refused to allow them meaningful possession.

After Anderson's dismissal, bad memories were revisited as England were forced into a rearguard action, but any other result than the one that was eventually delivered would have been a huge injustice.

England survived 29 nervous minutes, including added time, to make a powerful statement about their current status, which is much healthier than when recriminations about Tuchel's approach provided the post-World Cup narrative.

"I'm very impressed with the steps that we took after the World Cup", said Tuchel. "We wanted to get better, better in a deep build-up, get better in defending in a low block and, on top of it, we wanted always to impose our identity and the way we want to play against every opponent.

"I think this was clearly visible throughout the whole group phase. The results followed with an excellent group phase."

Was this the finest performance of Tuchel's time in charge? Most observers felt so, but the head coach was best placed to answer.

"Yes, given the circumstances," he said, "and the pressure, the quality, where we played in this building against the reigning world champions, unbeaten in 43 matches. Putting a performance out there in Madrid, and in this environment, was a very complete performance."

Tuchel will, of course, need repeat performances - but the outstanding ability and character England displayed here to beat the World Cup holders will deliver a huge injection of confidence and self-belief.

#894. Lye, Peterborough and the never-ending Women's FA Cup tie

Most of the second-round ties in the 2026-27 Women's FA Cup took place on Sunday

In years gone by, it was not unusual for FA Cup ties to require three attempts to complete as every drawn match would require another replay.

Nowadays, Women's FA Cup ties are decided on the day with extra time and penalties if needed.

Unless that tie is Lye Town v Peterborough United in the first round of the 2026-27 competition.

The match between the Women's National League sides has now been abandoned twice, and is yet to be completed.

The first go was abandoned because of a serious player injury, while the second on Sunday was called off amid bad weather.

It means that while most teams remaining in the competition are awaiting the third-round draw on Monday evening - when second-tier WSL2 sides enter the competition - Lye and Peterborough are still stuck in round one.

Fourth-tier Lye, of National League Division One Midlands, already had an unusual path to round one to face Peterborough of the National League Northern Premier, a division above.

Entering in the third qualifying round, their match against Coton Green was also postponed, so took place on October 22, after the first-round draw had been made.

A 5-0 win set up the Peterborough tie, due to be played on 8 November, a week after the other games.

It finally looked like the tie would be played to a conclusion as Lye led 1-0 with 12 minutes remaining.

But after a serious injury suffered by Lye goalkeeper Pharyn Ashton the match was abandoned and rescheduled again for 15 November.

This too proved in vain. Sunday's match was abandoned at half-time with Peterborough leading 3-1, because of a waterlogged pitch.

Spare a thought too for Rugby Borough, who are lined up to play the winner in round two but are also being forced to wait.

#892. Is academia’s risk-averse culture stifling scientific discovery?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Dom Byrne is a freelance radio and podcast producer based in Brighton, UK.

Your browser does not support the audio element.Download MP3See transcript

Nessa Carey's career has straddled both academia and industry. “In industry you tend to have much more of a sense of shared purpose, and you operate in teams,” she says.

Academia, on the other hand, is more personality-driven, and feels more individualistic. “Failure tends to be very binary: you either failed or you succeeded, and it's very personal,” she adds.

But as global research collaborations become more multidisciplinary, a culture change is needed in higher education, says Carey, who now runs a training business that supports biotechnology and drug discovery spinoffs.

Earlier this year, Carey spoke at a one-day conference on failure in science, with a focus on careers and innovation. It was held at Imperial College London in partnership with Nature.

In the penultimate episode of a six-part podcast series that revisits some of the conference themes, Carey urges academia to look at how industry handles failure, where struggling projects are abandoned more quickly.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03772-y

Is innovation as slow as it's often labelled?

Oftentimes we talk about innovation being slow, but in fact, you know, many of us feel like we're living in an ever-changing society.

After the failure and innovation session, the chair, Dr Nejra van Zalk, a design psychologist at Imperial College London, reported back to delegates attending the Failure in Science Conference, held in April this year.

[Recording from the Failure In Science conference]

Why do we choose innovation in one area of healthcare, for example, and not in another area? And who makes those decisions?

Why do we focus on obesity drugs and pump money into that, rather than helping to fix musculoskeletal issues in children who would have much better outcomes over a lifetime.

I'm Dr Stephen Webster, director of The Good Science Project at Imperial College London, a programme that examines what we like about research culture, and what we don't.

And in episode five of this series, we explore the business of discovery.

To put it bluntly, when it comes to failure, could universities learn a thing or two from industry?

[Recording from the Failure In Science conference]

How can we safely incorporate failure into our working models?

Can we look to industry to see how they're doing it when they actually, they cut their losses sooner and they abandon projects quicker and they can quantify their risks in different ways than we can in academia.

So my name is Nessa Carey, I'm a PhD scientist. And I've worked in academia, in industry, and as a freelancer. So I've kind of done a lot of things over the space of my career.

Oh, so so many failures. I started out with the classic academic failures of having grants rejected, having papers rejected.

In industry, you get things like programmes that you simply can't keep running. And also if you move to industry, you will be made redundant at some point or another.

And it's very easy, particularly the first time, to view that as a personal failure, but as you get more experienced, you realize it's just about organizations, it's just about shifting priorities, and actually it's not that big a deal.

So your definition of failure changes as your career changes. And also as you get older, I think it changes as well.

[Recording from the Failure In Science Conference]

I wanted to ask us, and perhaps ask the panel: as society, and this is not simply a UK perspective I don't think, have we become hyper risk averse?

Is that the direction that we're heading in?

And if so, where is the space for failure, and particularly the space for failure in science?

So, in the opening session of the conference at Imperial College, Professor Jem Woods suggested that we have become too risk averse and that that has really negative consequences, for example in academia.

And I think I absolutely agree with that, but I don't think it's just academia that is negatively impacted by this.

And I think the conversation has shifted, and not necessarily in a way that's helpful. And I think it's particularly a lot of pressure on younger people.

So I do quite a lot of outreach work in schools, and I see young students who are under enormous pressure to do well at their GCSEs or their A levels or whatever is the equivalent in another country, because they have to get onto the right course at the right college. They have to get a career trajectory that's working in the right direction.

And so I think there's a much bigger fear of failure because the stakes have been made artificially high.

In reality, as long as you do a course that you're happy on at a university where you're happy living, you'll do fine.

But we've built in this terrible sequential success demand on the young, and I think it's also exacerbated by [the fact we] we now have much more public discourse because we have social media, and everybody posts their triumphs. Everybody posts their success. You look at LinkedIn, and it's just full of people celebrating their promotion, their latest certificate, etc.

The trouble is that's not real. That's not how life generally progresses. You try stuff, you stuff up, you learn from it, and you move on.

And if we always class that as failure rather than a normal part of learning, then I think we do create really, really big problems for the future because everybody will try and stay inside their comfort zone.

Everybody will be frightened of doing something wrong.

It's a big problem in science because science thrives on innovation, but it's a big problem in any creative sector, and we run the risk of situations where people would rather do nothing than take a risk.

And you see that in organizations as well, and that's a really big problem.

I think what academia could do with learning from industry in terms of failure is to depersonalize it somewhat.

I think that's extremely difficult to do in reality.

One of the things that I enjoyed about working in industry, as opposed to working in academia, is in industry you tend to have much more of a sense of shared purpose, and you operate in teams. And yes, you may be the leader of a team, but you're still a team.

Academia, I find generally is much more individualistic.

If you have a much more individualistic environment, it is much harder to acknowledge failure as being simply a consequence of good decisions that are made by a team.

In academia, failure tends to be very binary: you either failed or you succeeded, and it's very personal. And it's very personal, in particular, to the Principal Investigators.

In industry, you can be doing really interesting work on a project, and then you do the killer experiment and realize your project can't go anywhere. And as a team, and as the leader of a team, you make the decision that that project needs to be terminated.

Now, that in academia would feel like failure because you can't then go on and apply for grants for it.

In industry, there's much more an emphasis in good companies on “did we make the right decision?”, and if you made the right decision, then the target failed or the program failed, but you didn't necessarily fail as an individual.

And I think it's that difference between viewing things as projects and teams and viewing things as individual endeavours.

And given that more and more science is becoming multidisciplinary, multi-team, it would make so much more sense if academia could start to change its culture towards that, because on the whole, the big papers that we see coming out now – they're big team efforts, and yet reward still tends to remain very individual.

So it's a structural issue. It's not just about people.

I think academia could adapt well by adopting some of the good managerial and people development skills of industry.

Academia is, in my experience, much more driven by personalities, and that creates enormous emotional heft behind things.

In industry, of course, there are big personalities. There are in every sector, but because you're working as an organization, you don't have quite this same strange mix of your personal emotional life with your professional life, and so you can fail professionally without it having quite the same impact on you as an individual emotionally, if that makes sense.

Something that the industry has got very, very good on is identifying killer experiments, carrying them out, and doing the thing that is considered a cliche now – but is absolutely critical – of fail fast, fail quickly, fail early, fail cheaply: that you don't keep trying to progress something that cannot get to the end point that you need.

And I think industry, on the whole, is very good at that. It used to be very bad. It's got better.

Academia is terrible at that in my experience, in that what will happen is somebody has their favourite target, their favourite process, their favourite enzyme, and they just keep working on it because they have a reputation for that and because they can keep working on it, rather than thinking “do you know what? It'd be really good to set up this experiment, see if I'm on the right track, and if I'm not, I'll kill it.” Instead, what they tend to do is just find other things they can keep working on in the same field.

Now, sometimes that's entirely appropriate, and sometimes it's that real curiosity-led stuff that takes us in a weird direction and opens up all sorts of things.

But there is always a risk that you will just keep chugging away at something because you know you'll at least get a couple of papers out of it, or because your PhD student needs the data for their thesis, etc.

It's a very different environment, and so it's not that I'm saying we should import everything from industry into academia, but I do think sometimes academia could benefit from the critical thinking of industry that goes: take away the emotion and actually look at this from scratch and say, “would we carry on if we were starting now?”

[Recording from the Failure In Science Conference]

So I mentioned these grand challenges; We often talk about them in science circles, The grand challenges. What's the role of science in helping society address these grand challenges?

And the emergence of innovation in technologies, I think has now switched to hyper disruptive technologies, and that's specifically around how we manage, or [how] information is managed. (When I say we, maybe it's not managed).

And then societal and community and individual access to those innovations in technology, and I think it's often labelled as ‘The BBC's Post-Truth Society’, because there were many of the BBC journalists (and some of them may be in the audience I don't know) who talked a lot about this emergence of that technological system in the post-truth society. And we have real questions in science to answer around that understanding of the way that information is generated and the way it's perceived and used societally.

So, in the opening session, Jem Woods was talking about the fact that there's been a drop of trust in science, and I wouldn't say it's just science.

There's a drop in trust in multiple areas, including in our trust in politicians, and our trust in writers, and our trust in the media.

And I think it's phenomenally important that scientists continue to do their work to the highest level of probity, and the vast majority of scientists do that, and that is true whatever sector you're in.

Scientists are remarkably similar, whether they're in academia or they're in industry; they're there because they want to do good science.

I think it's vital that everybody continues to do really good science. I think it's also vital, though, that we do challenge one another appropriately and professionally.

But what is also really important is that scientists continue to communicate, to a wider public, what is important about science and the scientific method, and also to be very upfront about the limitations of our research and the limitations of our findings.

This again, I think, ties into the issue of success and failure, because one of the things that's happened is public engagement and communication of science have been added to the academic workload.

The academic workload never decreases; new stuff always gets added to it, and it becomes another box to tick.

And there is a risk that people not only need to do good science, but they need to do science that can be communicated well.

And I think the most dangerous thing for academia is that it's constantly under pressure to justify why its science is being done. What is the benefit, the direct, very tangible benefit for humanity?

And that creates pressure to overstate one's outcomes, to be too black and white about it because black and white stories sell – it's much easier to sell a black and white story – but we have to be really careful not to do that because every time we do that and get challenged, we undermine the faith not so much in our science, because each member of the public has probably forgotten us, but the faith in science itself.

We shouldn't be scared of saying it's complicated, and so I think there is a real risk there that by being unsubtle about how we communicate our science, we actually undermine faith in a field which has essentially added enormous benefit to humanity and to the planet, and we need to be very careful not to lose that.

So I've worked in the field of innovation for about 25 years, and it's just as difficult now as it was 25 years ago.

But I think there are particular issues now that we're facing as a world that we didn't face back then. AI is the obvious one of having created a technology that actually may outrun us, and no one's quite clear how that's going to play out now.

But I think there are bigger issues at stake here as well.

I think it's very difficult when so much science is being published and being done to work out which of it genuinely has the potential to shift the needle on a particular issue.

But I think it's actually at risk of us having such a focus on innovation, in the sense of ‘where's the next great widget? Where's the next great drug?’, that we forget that technological innovation may not actually be what we require to solve particular problems.

So one of the things that really really frustrates me is seeing more and more emphasis, and more and more funding, in climate change going into carbon capture.

Carbon capture at scale is an entirely unproven technology, and it's not clear at all that it can solve the climate change problem.

We do, however, know that moving to electric cars makes a huge difference, and yet we are not in the UK legislating to do that appropriately.

We also have a situation where drug companies are spending billions of dollars to develop drugs for chronic health conditions that we actually know are caused essentially by social inequality and poverty.

We would be so much better as societies if we would put our money into more equitable healthcare systems, more equitable food availability systems.

We would have an enormous return on investment, but we don't see that return on investment for a very long time, and it's not a capitalist return on investment, it's a government return on investment.

So my concern is that our biggest failures will come because we constantly try to ‘tech’ our way out of problems that don't actually require technological solutions.

They require different, longer-term, less glossy solutions that don't make money for companies, and our systems on the whole run in a way that have placed an awful lot of, say, healthcare and environmental responsibilities and opportunities on big capitalist companies, when actually they are not the right structure to deliver those outcomes.

So that is where I think our biggest failures will come: We will ‘tech’ when we shouldn't be ‘tech-ing’. We will try and ‘tech’ very expensively when actually we could have made smaller investments with much more impact.

And it is deeply frustrating to me that also we as scientists will go “don't worry, we'll come up with a technological solution.” instead of saying “we may never come up with a technological solution, but if you talk to our friends in the social sciences, they already know what needs to be done. Why on earth aren't you doing this?” And that, I think, is a failure on the part of science to pretend that we are the ones who will solve everything.
