#891. More than F1 - Monza's captivating football story

Monza were formed in 1912 but did not play in Serie A for the first time until 2022

Think Monza, and the mind conjures up famous winning drives by Lewis Hamilton and Michael Schumacher, and by Kimi Antonelli this year on the way to his first Formula 1 title.

Sporting theatre on four wheels is not all that this northern Italian city has to offer, though.

Just under four miles from the historic home of motor racing's Italian Grand Prix sits the 17,000-capacity Stadio Brianteo, home to Serie A football club AC Monza.

It's not easy for the club to capture attention, given European giants AC Milan and Inter Milan play at the San Siro, a 20-minute drive away, while the romantic lure of Como is less than an hour from here by train.

But Monza have their own captivating story to tell.

Founded in 1912, the Biancorossi - white and reds - did not even play in Serie B for the first time until 1951. As recently as 2017, they were playing part-time in Serie D.

Under the guidance of former player Giovanni Stroppa, Monza were promoted to Serie A for the first time in 2022. Stroppa was sacked after a slow start in the top flight, but Monza survived for three years before being relegated.

They then bounced back immediately, earning their place among the elite again in May of this year.

Now owned by American venture capitalists Beckett Layne Ventures (BLV), and with former Southampton boss Ivan Juric in the manager's chair, Monza have a clear vision for how they can make an impact in their crowded geographical market.

AC Monza have played at the 17,000-capacity Stadio Brianteo since 1988

I am speaking to Monza chief executive Mauro Baldissoni in an office at the Stadio Brianteo, having been given a brief tour of the club's training facilities at Monzello, less than a five-minute drive away.

The atmosphere is positive after a 4-0 win over Cagliari the previous night - the club's biggest ever Serie A victory.

Monza sit third bottom at the time of writing, a point from safety, but the club feel so much is in their favour.

"First off, Monza is on the outskirts of Milan, so the location is attractive for the players," says Baldissoni. "It's a good point of visibility for what we do.

"There is a point of attraction and point of awareness about Monza, because it is already known in the world for luxury sports through the association with Formula 1.

"The infrastructure at the club is larger and probably more efficient than Milanello, the sporting centre of Milan, because they cannot have all the teams from the youngest in the academy to the first team like we can. This province specifically is one of the richest in terms of GDP in Europe.

"So, you have all the premises to create a good project. And there is always people coming to watch.

"Yesterday there were people from Newcastle, Fulham, Southampton, Sunderland, Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund at the game, and there were others. If you come here, you can watch AC Milan, Como, [an] Atalanta game, Inter game, and Monza.

"Scouts and sporting directors can come for two days and watch different games at a high level."

England youth international Jay Robinson (left) celebrates with striker Gustavo Varela during Monza's 4-0 win against Cagliari in October

Monza president Lauren Crampsie was previously the chief marketing officer at Chelsea.

She is now of the founders of BLV, which paid â¬45m to the family of the late Silvio Berlusconi to buy up Monza.

Crampsie, 46, watched the pre-match build-up from the pitch before the Cagliari win, making sure all the details were in order. Afterwards, she is mindful to let the players and coaching staff enjoy their victory.

Young striker Gustavo Varela is the star of the night, scoring two of his 11 goals in all competitions so far this season, earning himself a first senior call-up to the Portugal squad.

Monza paid Benfica Â£2.5m for the 21-year-old, who is currently top scorer in Serie A, with nine in nine games.

Already there are big-name suitors sniffing around, doubtless willing to pay a fee significantly higher than the one Monza forked out.

It is a perfect illustration of the business model the club are trying to create.

"We always think the club's mission is to win games, but it is also about forming players that are part of their academy first and also trying to identify talents that can fit with the purposes and the style of the club," says Baldissoni, who spent 10 years with Roma before leaving in 2020.

"In Rome we were able to identify young talents like Marquinhos, who was 18 years old and able to play as a starter before we sold him to Paris St-Germain.

"There were others like Erik Lamela and Mo Salah. But in Rome it is more difficult because expectations are higher.

"In Monza the idea is the same. The pressure is bigger because the impact of relegation on revenues is worse. But the environment and the sporting expectations are more manageable for a young player who has more time to form his emotional background."

Monza fought off competition from League One club Leicester to sign Southampton's England youth international Jay Robinson on loan this season, with Juric's presence being key.

The 19-year-old has already played 10 times in all competitions, scoring twice.

The main entrance of Monza's training ground

Fiorentina, Roma, Como and Juventus provide a stiff run of fixtures for Monza heading towards Christmas, before an equally important match against Venezia, who are currently one place and one point worse off in the table.

Baldissoni is optimistic. His wider view of the football landscape is not altered by the knowledge that promoted Premier League trio Coventry, Hull and Ipswich all spent in excess of Â£120m in the summer, a figure Monza can only dream of.

Plans are under way to refurbish Stadio Brianteo, which has covering over a single stand.

"Infrastructure is the weakest point in Italy under the competition point of view, to compete with other global markets," Baldissoni says.

"But there are costs and there are investments."

He says the stadium is "an investment meant to generate more revenues".

"Of course, the Premier League's revenues are much higher than all the other leagues, so those clubs have a competitive advantage.

"But they also overpay players because it's Premier League. Maybe they get a player that I would like to have because they can pay more, but maybe I can find another player that is not that far away. Then you have to be able to form the player.

"So, you identify a talent early, and then you keep forming him to bring him to a level where some other players already are. Maybe then we sell him to Premier League?"

It's a delicate balancing act, but Monza are sure it can be done.

"Sassuolo made it to Serie A 13 years ago for the first time and until last season, spent all that time in Serie A. Atalanta was going up and down and now it's one of the prominent teams, targeting European competitions every year," Baldissoni says.

"This is out of the work they've been doing in terms of identifying talents, forming talents, and remaining competitive.

"That is the target. It is possible. Let's see if we can make it."

#890. Bulgaria highway pileup kills 12, dozens injured: PM

At least 12 people were killed and dozens injured in a series of crashes caused by thick fog in Bulgaria. Police, firefighters and paramedics were dispatched to the scene for the rescue operation.

At least 12 people have been killed and dozens more injured in a series of crashes on both sides of a highway in Bulgaria on Tuesday, Bulgarian authorities said.

According to the interior ministry, a bus and truck collided, leading to a pileup on the side of the A1 highway near the southeastern city of Yambol.

Speaking to reporters at the site, ministry's general secretary Ministry Lyubomir Nikolov said that fog was likely the cause of the accident.

The regional governor of Yambol Georgi Chalakov, said an estimated 50 cars and trucks were involved in the accident.

Health Minister Katya Ivkova said 10 people “died on the spot” and two others died while being transported to a hospital. She said 46 people were also injured and transported to medical facilities.

Prime Minister Rumen Radev, who was welcoming European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, cleared his schedule for later Tuesday. Von der Leyen said she would cut her ​visit short.

Police, firefighters and paramedics were dispatched to the scene on the A1 highway connecting the capital Sofia to the Black Sea city of Burgas.

Chief Inspector ⁠Todor Mishinev from the Yambol Regional Directorate of the Ministry of Internal Affairs ⁠told Nova TV that people were still trapped in their cars at the time of speaking.

"Right now, the priority is rescue operations. Once they are completed, the procedural and investigative actions will be carried out," he said.

The injured were being taken to hospitals in nearby cities, while authorities dispatched two aircraft carrying medical teams and stretcher equipment.

Bulgaria saw 71 road fatalities per million inhabitants in 2025, the highest rate in the European Union, according to European Commission figures. For orientation, EU average is 43 per million.

Victims say reckless driving, neglected road infrastructure and an inefficient justice system contribute to the country's high number of fatal traffic accidents.

#889. South Africa Rugby condemns online abuse of officials after Erasmus ban

South Africa condemn online abuse of World Rugby officials following Rassie Erasmus six-Test ban; Springboks head coach received suspension for comments following Nations Championship defeat to France, claiming 'match-fixing' and more; SA Rugby has requested full misconduct hearing

South Africa Rugby has condemned online abuse of World Rugby officials following the decision to hand Springboks coach Rassie Erasmus a six-match ban.

An independent panel imposed the punishment after reviewing comments made by Erasmus at a media conference on Monday ahead of the Nations Championship match against Ireland at the Aviva Stadium on Saturday.

SA Rugby has requested a full misconduct hearing for the 54-year-old, who will not be able to have any matchday involvement in international fixtures during the suspension.

Erasmus delivered an outspoken press conference on Monday, in which he suggested officials had missed 17 illegal tackles against his side during their crunch Nations Championship clash. He went as far as questioning whether "match-fixing" and "manipulation" of the result was behind why those incidents were not picked up.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

World Rugby confirmed it had reviewed the comments made by Erasmus, and an independent panel had imposed the sanction under World Rugby's Match Official Abuse Sanction Process, a framework that was introduced in July.

Following a social media backlash against the global governing body, SA Rugby has called for calm to allow the proper processes to run their course.

"SA Rugby is aware of the extensive public commentary, analysis and debate surrounding recent matters involving Springbok head coach Rassie Erasmus and World Rugby," a statement from the organisation read.

"We are mindful that a significant volume of commentary, opinion and AI-generated content is currently circulating in the public domain, much of which does not necessarily reflect the facts, context or processes involved.

"What is deeply concerning, however, is the reaction of some individuals on social media and other platforms, particularly reports of threats and abusive conduct directed at World Rugby officials and administrators.

"SA Rugby unequivocally condemns any form of intimidation, threats or personal attacks. Such behaviour has no place in rugby and is entirely contrary to the values upon which our game is founded.

"Rugby has long been recognised as a sport built on respect, discipline, integrity and sportsmanship. These values extend beyond the field of play and apply equally to players, coaches, match officials, administrators and supporters. While robust debate and differing opinions are part of sport, they must always be expressed respectfully and responsibly.

"SA Rugby also wishes to assure all stakeholders that rugby possesses the necessary expertise, experience and governance structures to deal with matters of this nature appropriately.

"Any issues that arise will be addressed through the established rugby processes and by the individuals entrusted with these responsibilities, ensuring that due process is followed and that the best interests of the game remain paramount.

"We remain committed to protecting the integrity of rugby, upholding its values and ensuring that all participants in the game are treated with dignity and respect."

#887. How did England cling on against Spain and what did Tuchel do differently?

James Trafford (right) kept Spain out in the latter stages

England held on to beat Spain 3-2 with a backs-to-the-wall finale in the Nations League to finish top of their group.

But many observers would have been feeling a sense of deja vu from the World Cup semi-final when England sat back and were beaten by Argentina.

So what was different this time? BBC Sport has a look.

First of all the context of the two games was entirely different.

England were 1-0 up against Argentina in the 55th minute on neutral territory in Atlanta - and still had all their players.

Anthony Gordon had put them ahead but Lionel Messi set up Enzo Fernandez and then Lautaro Martinez late on.

But against Spain the best performance of Thomas Tuchel's reign had them 3-0 up through goals from Harry Kane, Ezri Konsa and Ben White.

Elliot Anderson then fouled Lamine Yamal for a penalty, which Mikel Oyarzabal scored - and that began the siege at a partisan Riyadh Air Metropolitano.

Nico Williams made it 3-2 but Spain could not find an equaliser, thanks in part to England keeper James Trafford.

"Half an hour feels like two hours against a team like this [with 10 men]," Tuchel told ITV afterwards. "That's the way it is. Without the red card we were clear winners."

60 minutes of perfection, 30 minutes of chaos - an England win for the ages

England cling on to stun world champions Spain in thriller

Making defensive subs is fine when it works - but when it does not, boy will a manager hear about it.

In the World Cup last 16, England had been 2-1 up against Mexico in the Azteca when Jarell Quansah was sent off.

Tuchel brought on three defenders for a defender, a midfielder and a forward.

But England won 3-2 and Dan Burn's cameo was the stuff of legend.

However, nine days later with England 1-0 up against Argentina, Tuchel did the same again - three defenders on for a defender, midfielder and forward.

The first of those subs, with Konsa replacing Anthony Gordon, was in the 72nd minute.

And England just sat back until Argentina broke their resistance.

However, against Spain this time, despite England being down to 10 men and facing incessant pressure, Tuchel was not so quick with defensive subs.

Myles Lewis-Skelly, replacing Harry Kane, was the first on after 78 minutes - 15 minutes after Anderson's sending off. And then five minutes later he brought on two more players - but one of them was a striker in Dominic Calvert-Lewin.

Burn replaced fellow defender White in the 89th minute.

"Harry played 78 minutes, Jude [Bellingham] 83 minutes and then just defending and defending, it's tiring," explained Tuchel.

"So we needed fresh energy. I was asked yesterday what happens if there needs to be a critical or crucial substitution. And I said, I feel free enough to take any substitution if I think it is necessary to help the team and to influence the game.

"I feel free enough to do that and I think there was a lot of defending needed. So we just went for some fresh legs."

Win over world champions Spain is a 'statement' - Tuchel

England actually faced more of a siege this time than against the Argentines, the stats confirm.

In the final 30 minutes they faced 19 shots from Spain, with seven on target and an expected goals (xG) total of 2.53.

Argentina, in that time, had 10 shots, with four on target and an xG of 1.41.

In terms of passes from England the numbers were similar with 65 against Argentina and 61 against Spain - both times with an accuracy rate of about 64%.

In Thursday's 2-1 win against Croatia, as a comparison, they tried 557 passes with accuracy of 89%.

"For half an hour it was Mexico reloaded and it felt like we were back in the Azteca. We had to overcome 30 minutes which, against Spain, felt like three hours," Tuchel told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"The difficult thing is it's not only a red card, it's a red card, and a goal so that makes a completely new game. Thirty minutes against the world champion feels like three hours. I said it before in the stadium and wave after wave after wave."

England were criticised for blowing a 2-1 half-time lead at Wembley in their first Nations League game with Spain.

But on that day their final 30-minute figurers were much better - with only five shots faced and 176 attempted passes with a 90% accuracy.

So what was different this time? Perhaps the team showed more resilience and unity?

After Spain had pulled one back England's players had a huddle.

"I love the fact the team went into a huddle and if anything the manager's stepped back because he wants to see the player reaction," said ex-England defender Matt Upson on BBC Radio 5 Live.

"I almost think that the trauma from that sending off of Elliot Anderson has almost been a positive thing for England because it's given the team a chance to get together and cope in what is an incredibly difficult situation and come through the other side.

"There was so much going on in this game. England had to suffer and came through the other side."

Defender and goalscorer White was asked about the huddle after the game.

"Just stay calm, when you're one down it becomes more difficult and things change so it was all about managing that," he said.

Another factor was the performance of England keeper James Trafford, who made six saves - with four of them coming in the final 12 minutes of the game with the score at 3-2.

He made an incredible double save to deny Fermin Lopez and Lamine Yamal in injury time.

Upson said: "I think that double save was the moment for Spain and Trafford had the answers."

#885. Piastri to serve grid penalty at Las Vegas GP

Oscar Piastri will serve a grid penalty in Las Vegas; McLaren confirm upgraded floor to be added to MCL40 at late stage of season; watch the Las Vegas GP weekend on Sky Sports F1, with qualifying at 4am on Saturday and the race at 4am on Sunday

McLaren have confirmed that Oscar Piastri will serve a 10-place grid penalty at this weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix as he will be forced to exceed his engine allowance for the season.

Following an unspecified reliability issue, Piastri will need to use his fifth Internal Combustion Engine (ICE) of the season, taking him beyond the limit of four that each driver has for the season.

A team statement said: "Oscar will take a new Internal Combustion Engine in Las Vegas after a reliability issue.

"As it is his fifth of the season, he will take a 10-place grid penalty, but he has a good chance to recover positions with overtaking in Saturday's race."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

The Las Vegas Strip Circuit features a 1.2-mile straight that drivers take flat out, which should present a good opportunity for Piastri to surge back through the field.

McLaren also confirmed that both Piastri and his team-mate Lando Norris will have their cars fitted with a new turbo specification, which has been made available by the power unit supplier Mercedes following an engine upgrade.

"Both cars, as with the other HPP-powered cars, will be fitted with a new ADUO-enabled turbo specification," the team added. "The expected performance benefit is relatively small."

Las Vegas GP: What's still to play for over final three races of F1 2026 season with battles in drivers' and constructors' championships

Mercedes confirm ADUO turbo upgrade ready for Las Vegas GP with Kimi Antonelli set to run new engine part

F1 news, rumours and gossip: Formula 1 latest updates on teams, driver transfer market and contracts

Las Vegas GP: What happens in Vegas... Celebs causing CARNAGE

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Despite there being just three rounds remaining of the 2026 season, McLaren will continue to upgrade their car with a new floor arriving in time for Las Vegas.

Having officially been dethroned as constructors' champions by Mercedes last time out in Brazil, McLaren are attempting to close down a 17-point deficit to Red Bull in the battle for third in this year's standings.

A McLaren statement said: "The team will bring further developments to the MCL40 as they continue to push to unlock more performance in the remaining races, primarily a new floor.

"We will also have some solutions to improve drag during the Free Practice sessions, which we will then review before making a decision on whether to run them on Friday.

"With plenty of opportunities to exploit the car's potential, both through evaluating the new upgrades and refining how to operate the package at the maximum potential available, the priority is to turn those learnings into performance on track and valuable points in the immediate term."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

McLaren were the only member of F1's 'big four' teams to bring upgrades to Brazil, where the new parts helped Norris win the Sao Paulo Grand Prix.

Ross Hood, McLaren executive director of programme delivery, said: "Our programme delivery has evolved throughout this year and continues to do so.

"The new regulations, combined with the volume and pace of performance coming from the tunnel and engineering through to the circuit, have made it an intense year. That galvanises the team and brings us closer together, so we get the right performance to the track while challenging each other and our ideas.

"A new floor is arriving in Las Vegas this week, and it's a great example of our programme delivery. The collaboration between Aerodynamics, Design, Performance, Planning and Manufacturing helped ensure the team could maximise the output of the last tunnel runs for the 40A. It's a big push, but by making decisions closely together, we hit the targets we set ourselves."

#884. Has Trafford replaced Pickford as England No 1?

James Trafford has made five appearances for England, all of them in 2026

As he was mobbed by his England team-mates for a late double save that secured a memorable 3-2 win against world champions Spain, the debate that followed about who the country's number one is was inevitable.

The Leeds keeper was given his chance to show England boss Thomas Tuchel what he could do again - and he absolutely took it.

On his fifth England cap the 24-year-old enjoyed a magnificent performance in Madrid as his side handed the hosts their first loss in 43 matches.

Trafford made four key saves in the final 12 minutes of the game, including an incredible double stop to first deny a Lamine Yamal curler and then dive again to his right to keep out Fermin Lopez from close range.

Last week Tuchel had made it clear that Everton goalkeeper Jordan Pickford was his number one.

But after full-time in Spain Tuchel told ITV Sport "there's no number one" and Trafford had "a brilliant match".

So, following his performance on Sunday night, is Trafford now likely to oust Pickford as England's go-to goalkeeper?

Is Trafford 'closing the gap' on Pickford?

Despite being just 24 years old Trafford has already been England's most expensive goalkeeper by transfer fee... twice.

Trafford returned to his boyhood Manchester City from Burnley for a Â£31m fee in 2025 and then left the Etihad for Leeds for Â£45m this summer - having been limited to being Pep Guardiola's 'cup goalkeeper'.

Given the downturn in form of their current goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma, many City fans may well be wishing Trafford had stayed. Their loss is Leeds' - and maybe England's - gain.

At Leeds he has found his form and this season ranks first among the 52 goalkeepers who have played at least 10 games in Europe's big five leagues by save percentage (81.4%).

He has made five appearances for England, all of them in 2026, and has rotated with Pickford across the Three Lions' five matches since the World Cup.

Pickford has started against Czech Republic and Croatia twice whereas Trafford has played against Czech Republic and started both England's matches with Spain, home and away.

After England's win in Madrid, which was the first time Spain had lost in the city in 39 years, Trafford's double-save was praised by his Three Lions team-mate Declan Rice.

"Everything happened so quick so for him to make two in the space of two seconds is massive," he told ITV. "A massive night for him."

Spain manager Luis de la Fuente agreed. He said: "We did generate some chances but England's goalkeeper has produced a fantastic performance and stopped two or three potential goals in the last 10 or 15 minutes."

After the double-save several England players ran over to celebrate with Trafford.

And on Tuchel's decision to rotate between his two keepers former Manchester United captain Roy Keane told ITV: "I think it's smart management.

"This is the perfect time for Trafford to come in, against top players, and show what he's capable of doing."

Social media has been full of the 'England number one' debate since, with many suggesting this was a moment that marked the changing of the guard.

Could Tuchel really now not start with Trafford for England's Nations League quarter-finals? Only time will tell.

What about Pickford though? England's undisputed first choice for almost 10 years has rarely let his country down.

The 32-year-old has won 94 caps for England since making his debut in a 0-0 draw with Germany in 2017 and during his time as number one England have reached two World Cup semi-finals and two Euros finals.

According to Opta stats, Pickford has only made two errors leading to goals across his England career, with 46 clean sheets and a 74.3% save ratio.

And since the start of the 2024-25 season, only Arsenal's title-winning keeper David Raya has more clean sheets in the league than Pickford at Everton.

"We saw the last selections and all thought Jordan Pickford's place is under threat and James Trafford is going to be the next number one. I don't think Thomas Tuchel saw it as starkly or simply as that," said former England number one goalkeeper Paul Robinson to BBC Sport before England's win against Spain,

"It's a conversation that will definitely take place down the road, but not now. Jordan is England's first choice, in my opinion, rightfully so given his consistency and performances over such a long period.

"This is a debate and conversation for the future definitely because Father Time catches up with everyone eventually and the manager needs to have a contingency plan, but Jordan Pickford very much remains number one and Thomas Tuchel has said as much.

"I don't think Jordan Pickford is under threat for his jersey on a permanent basis any time soon, irrespective of the next selection."

This isn't a debate that is going away any time soon. But having two goalkeepers genuinely competing for that number one shirt can only be to England's benefit.

#883. WSL talking points: Chelsea’s gamble pays off and have Arsenal lost fear factor?

Blues beat champions after bold substitution and Gunners’ home struggles continue with fifth consecutive WSL draw

Sonia Bompastor attempted to deflect suggestions that the removal of Kadeisha Buchanan 12 minutes into Chelsea’s top-of-the-table clash with Manchester City was tactical, but few were convinced by the claim that it was down to injury. The manager said the centre-back, who had not asked to come off and walked straight down the tunnel, had taken a knock to the head in training and been assessed and cleared, but that during the game “she was not herself”. On came Veerle Buurman and the threat of Khadija Shaw was nullified, the Dutch defender restricting the golden boot favourite so well that Shaw did not manage a shot on target. Bompastor said after the game that she had not spoken to Buchanan but that she would “explain myself to her”. “I always have good relationships with the players, bring them clarity, and I’m always direct and honest so they have the information,” she said. “It won’t be any different.” Enforced or not, the substitution was a huge gamble that paid off, even after the loss of Melvine Malard to injury in the first half reduced their number of remaining in-game substitution windows to one. Suzanne Wrack

Match report: Chelsea 1-0 Manchester City

Manchester United earned their fourth clean sheet in all competitions in their 2-0 defeat of Crystal Palace. Maya Le Tissier stole the headlines with her goal on her 150th appearance for the club but the team’s improved defensive stability is also catching the eye and the centre-back is key to that. “For a defender you expect as the minimum you need to defend well and help to build,” said the head coach, Eva Olid. “But now she’s scoring goals and that is more than a manager can ask from a centre-back. She’s in a high level and I’m so happy for her.” Le Tissier is showing consistent solidity and appears to be enjoying life under Olid now that things have settled, after seven goals conceded in their opening two WSL games. United have conceded four in eight WSL games since and are starting to show their flair. SW

Have teams stopped fearing Arsenal at the Emirates Stadium? Their run of five consecutive WSL draws at home suggests so. London City Lionesses had 56% possession on Sunday and controlled the game for significant spells, especially in the second half, and although Arsenal created the greater chances, they do not play with the aura of a side attracting the largest attendances in the division. Renée Slegers was asked whether she was worried her team were losing that home “fear factor” and said: “No, because we love playing at the Emirates. We had the biggest crowd so far in the season, the atmosphere was fantastic under the lights.” Probed further about her side’s home form, the head coach said: “I don’t think we’ve lost the fear factor, I think it’s a very hard place for oppositions to come.” Her side host West Ham next Sunday, looking for that elusive home WSL win. Tom Garry

Tottenham Hotspur were the latest team frustrated by Everton’s defensive solidity as they were held to a goalless draw. Despite controlling the ball and registering 17 shots, only three efforts were on target as they failed to score for the first time. Martin Ho was keen to highlight their opponents’ strengths as a key reason. “When we got into that attacking third, it was going to take something really special,” he told Spursplay. “They defended so deep with so many numbers behind the ball. You’re waiting for one of those moments to drop.” It was just the kind of performance fans have come to expect from Scott Phelan’s side. Unbeaten in their past three, in which they have faced Manchester United, Chelsea and Spurs, Everton have developed a strong resilience and character in recent weeks. Where they struggle is at the other end. Everton have scored eight goals this season (three of them own goals), higher than only Charlton in the WSL. Sophie Downey

Liverpool ended their five-game winless league run with a statement victory over struggling Brighton, their third away win in 17 games. It has been a frustrating October and November block for Gareth Taylor and his team so there was much relief on the sideline that they were finally able to turn performance and opportunity into three points. Liverpool had less of the ball but their fast counterattacking proved too much for the Seagulls. A significant key to their success was Beata Olsson. She has six goals from her past five games in all competitions, stepping up when her team have needed it most. Injuries have kept out Aurélie Csillag and Ceri Holland for the best part of the season and Sophie Roman Haug is recovering from an anterior cruciate ligament injury sustained 13 months ago. With limited attacking options, therefore, it will be very welcome that the Swedish striker has found her form in front of goal. SD

Viviane Asseyi continued her impressive scoring form with a superb brace in West Ham’s 2-0 victory over Charlton, taking her WSL tally to seven this season. The striker opened the scoring with a composed finish from the edge of the area before producing the standout moment of the afternoon, curling a spectacular 25-yard free-kick into the top corner beyond Charlton’s goalkeeper, Anna Koivunen. Asseyi could have completed a hat-trick but her two goals proved decisive. West Ham’s head coach, Rita Guarino, described her as “an important player”, adding that Asseyi was in a good goalscoring spell. Guarino felt Asseyi could have been happier with a hat-trick, but her latest double underlines her importance to West Ham’s attacking threat. Mitul Samji

Poor officiating dominated the narrative of the second city derby as Aston Villa edged Birmingham City 1-0, with both sides feeling hard done by. First, City felt Lucy Parker had fouled Océane Hurtré in the penalty area in the 24th minute, only for the referee to award a corner. Whether the incident was inside the box was disputable, but it did appear to be a foul. Minutes later, Villa had a goal from Océane Deslandes overruled for what was declared a foul on the goalkeeper in another contentious call, but they managed to find a winner in the second half. The decisions added to growing concerns about consistency in the WSL. Ho recently suggested officiating had worsened, and matches such as this do little to ease those concerns. Before VAR is introduced, improving the quality of refereeing must be a priority to avoid undermining the league’s standards and progress. Réshma Rao

#882. Megaspeed and the battle to go high-end Nvidia chips into China

Jensen Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy has shone a light on Megaspeed, the company she worked for. It is under investigation in the US for smuggling Nvidia chips into China, which it denies.

As Nvidia, one of the world's most valuable companies, grapples with CEO Jensen Huang's romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese spy, attention is turning to the much smaller company she worked for.

Alice H., the alleged spy, worked as an executive for Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center and AI computing company. It manages data center access, including for some major Chinese tech firms such as Alibaba.

According to Megaspeed's website as of November 2026, the company advertises itself as an "Nvidia cloud partner", saying it provides "computing power product services covering Nvidia's entire GPU product line." GPU stands for Graphic Processing Unit, a specialized electronic circuit that are in high demand for artificial intelligence (AI) applications, because they are designed to handle high numbers of parallel mathematical calculations. Megaspeed says it provides access for clients to Nvidia's advanced GB200 NVL72 ​computing system.

This type of firm is often referred to as a "neocloud". It buys Nvidia chips and computing power and then rents it out — in this case, at multiple sites across south-east Asia, to different companies. The US has set up strict export controls to prevent that Nvidia's high-performance chips end up in China, because it sees China as a competitor in the global AI race. It also does not want data centers made up of Nvidia chips to be owned by Chinese companies. It does, however, tolerate that data center compute with Nvidia chips be rented out to Chinese companies like Alibaba, and occasionally allows the export of Nvidia chips for specific purposes.

Megaspeed has bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia's products in recent years and has been accused of breaching US export controls to divert Nvidia chips into China.

In December 2025, Bloomberg reported that the "once-obscure" Megaspeed had become the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in all of south-east Asia and that the US government was investigating its ownership structure and whether or not it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China.

At the same time, Singapore police began an investigation into whether or not Megaspeed had "violated local laws" without specifying which ones. Those investigations are believed to be still ongoing.

On December 23, 2025, Megaspeed strenuously denied any wrongdoing in a statement — which still appears as the first page for visitors to the company's website as of November 2026.

"There has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities, and this demonstrates that we are a compliant and legitimate company," it said. "We operate fully within the bounds of all applicable export control regulations and maintain the highest standards of legal and ethical conduct."

The US government investigation began in 2024. The Commerce Department initially began looking into Megaspeed, but the US Justice Department has since taken over. According to the New York Times, this switch came about after an Nvidia executive directly contacted the Commerce Department about the investigation.

Megaspeed was founded in 2015 and was originally called 7Road International. It changed its name to Megaspeed in March 2023. It is owned by the Singapore-registered Swiftdata, which was set up in October 2023.

Its rise in prominence coincided with a sharp increase in assets, which increased from $33 million in 2023 to $3 billion in 2024.

Alice H., the woman accused of being a Chinese spy, had an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. She is widely seen as an influential figurehead at Megaspeed. She also served as the company's managing director of Megaspeed for eight months in 2023.

The Financial Times reported on Monday that Alice H. leveraged her close access to Jensen Huang and Nvidia to pitch AI chips deals to Chinese investors.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The newspaper said that in early 2025, Alice H. sought investment in China for a data center project in south-east Asia, and cited their easy access to Nvidia chips and close relationship with Alibaba.

Alibaba lent money to Megaspeed in June 2024, via subsidiaries. It has remained Megaspeed's largest client, according to reporting by the Financial Times.

In December 2025, Nvidia said its own inquiry into Megaspeed had found no evidence of chips being diverted and that the company was fully owned and operated outside of China, with no Chinese shareholders. The company told Bloomberg at the time that it had visited Megaspeed's facilities on multiple occasions and had seen nothing untoward.

Megaspeed is one of several companies accused of smuggling Nvidia's chips into China or finding ways to give Chinese companies access to them.

Nvidia's high-performance chips are seen as essential for companies looking for the most advanced form of supercomputing to use and develop various AI applications.

Back in 2022, the Biden Administration began severely restricting the sale of the US's most advanced chips to China, part of the two countries' growing rivalry to achieve AI dominance.

However, an illegal smuggling and underground network was soon set up, with many vendors operating to get the chips into China and selling them on to companies there.

In December 2025, US authorities shut down the operations of Hao Global, a US-based shell company with links to China which plead guilty to smuggling Nvidia chips to China.

In June 2026, Taiwanese government agencies raided the offices of Super Micro Computer as part of an investigation into the smuggling of Nvidia chips to China.

While export restrictions have been eased significantly under the Trump administration, there are still significant blocks and restrictions on the most advanced Nvidia chips.

In December 2025, the Trump administration approved several Chinese companies to buy or handle advanced Nvidia H200 chips, a move that sparked significant concern among the US security establishment.

However, that deal has not led to a significant flow of Nvidia chips moving legally to China, amid strict US licencing controls and official reluctance from Beijing to publicly promote Nvidia chips to the detriment of its own alternatives.

#881. What's the story with Scotland boss Pocognoli - is it time to go?

A few short months ago, Craig Mulholland, the Scottish FA's chief football officer, and Ian Maxwell, the association's chief executive, spoke about the worldwide search for a new Scotland head coach.

The data, the metrics, the cosmic input from the analytics company whose input was received at Hampden as if written on tablets of stone.

The process all pointed to Sebastien Pocognoli being their guy. They paraded him around Hampden, told everybody that loads of clubs were on his tail but that they won the chase.

They may, or may not, have mentioned the word 'coup' but that was certainly what their body language was telling you.

For coup, read boo, the sound surely reverberating around the Tartan Army right now after Monday's 4-0 defeat by Switzerland.

Some nonsense has been written about Pocognoli being on twice the salary that Steve Clarke was on, but whatever they're paying him, there's no value in it so far.

Money is a factor here. Clarke's three qualifications brought a rich bounty into the SFA's coffers, many millions even after deductions. That cash gave the association a little more opportunity to do some of the things they want to do in grassroots football.

A world where Scotland miss out on major championships and the financial windfalls that come with qualification is not a place they want to revisit. The next Euros looks like a gimme - almost harder not to qualify than qualify - but the sense of drift in this team is alarming and can't go on much longer.

Mulholland, Maxwell and let's throw SFA president Mike Mulraney into the mix, should be feeling mightily nervous.

Pocognoli wants patience but Scotland 'don't have time' says Robertson

Pocognoli's abject Scotland suffer 4-0 Nations League defeat in Switzerland

Robertson eclipses Dalglish to become Scotland's most capped man

Most people understood that Pocognoli needed time, but implicit in that understanding was a need to see something developing under him, a burgeoning style of play, some positives here and there, a few signs that even though things might not be great today or tomorrow, they're inching in the right direction.

There's been none of that. Decent players look lost. Pocognoli's system has made Scotland a disjointed soft touch. Structural discipline collapses too often. Players charge forward and leave space in behind. He wants hard pressing and maximum intensity, but his players don't look capable of providing it.

In six games they have scored five goals - two from the penalty spot. Promises of jam tomorrow are not cutting it. People can see a team on the slide.

In Switzerland, there was a drubbing that piles the heat on the Belgian, on the people who appointed him and on the players, too.

'You do not have time in international football'

If the chaos on the field wasn't a bad enough look for Pocognoli, then some of the words said in the wake of this objectionable 4-0 pummelling to a Switzerland B side playing in third gear only made things worse.

Andy Robertson, on the night he became Scotland's most capped player in history, delivered a damning riff that sounded strongly like a commentary on this coaching regime and this set of players.

In his stead, John McGinn did much the same thing. "You don't get time" was the gist. Who doesn't get time?

Robertson and McGinn didn't lay it on the line, but their thoughts resembled distress flares. These Scotland players can be overhyped, but they are better than some of the nonsense they dished up in St Gallen.

More than one former Scotland international reckoned they saw players not exactly busting a gut out there. These guys know the tell-tale signs.

Some private conversations between the SFA hierarchy and the senior operators in this team need to take place. What were they suggesting in the post-match? What are they really thinking?

An honesty session behind closed doors needs to take place long before the qualification campaign for the next Euros begins in March.

Pocognoli comes across as a good person: open, communicative, passionate and hard-working.

He also appears stubborn in the way he sets up his team, a system that is so easily exploited by more experienced coaches, people like Switzerland boss Murat Yakin, who was missing a battalion of heavy hitters and yet still won this game at a canter.

Yakin started six players who had six caps or fewer to their name - three of them scored.

McGinn said later that Scotland were in this movie before in the early days of Clarke's tenure, mentioning the 4-0 loss to Russia in 2019 - four goals conceded in 27 minutes.

The difference between Clarke and Pocognoli is obvious. Clarke had vast experience and the nous to fix the problems. Pocognoli is a young coach with no such back story, no such track record in turning bad situations into good.

Pocognoli said later that people should look beyond the result, to the "attitude of the players" who were at times "brilliant, brave and on the front foot".

He argued that 4-0 wasn't a true reflection of the game, referring to the glaring misses by Lewis Ferguson and Scott McTominay. Scotland were 3-0 down at the time. He didn't think the loss had anything to do with a system or a lack of confidence or a lack of belief.

Not many fans were buying what he was selling. Listening to some of his players, you doubted that they were buying it either.

After the home loss to Slovenia, Robertson said his team had been "out-played" and "out-fought." There were some other comments made after the desperately stodgy 2-1 win over North Macedonia on Friday. On Monday, it cranked up another level.

McGinn was asked if he felt Scotland were on the right path. "Impossible for me to say yes," he replied. It was hard to listen to what the players were trying to say and conclude that everybody's on the same page in this set-up.

Intransigence is not a good characteristic for any manager. In recent times we've seen a few bosses at big clubs who were wedded to their principles. Russell Martin and Wilfried Nancy didn't last long at Rangers and Celtic.

To repeat Robertson's line, you don't get time.

Clarke had an instinctive understanding of that and pragmatism was his way of taking his team forward, difficult yard by difficult yard. Rigid idealism is not a sensible way to operate, but Pocognoli has gone down that road in his first six games.

It's a dead-end down there. He needs to turn back and find another way while he still can. If he still can.

'Scotland have not played well in any game this campaign'

#880. Echoes of Azteca but not like Argentina: fearless England start afresh in Madrid

‘We will not go back on this way of playing,’ says Thomas Tuchel after he delivered response to World Cup critics

Thomas Tuchel made defensive substitutions as England protected a lead. He finished with three centre-backs on the pitch. His team could not get out of their half in the final part of the game. So close your eyes and imagine an alternate universe in which James Trafford did not make his stunning double save in stoppage time on Sunday and England had drawn 3-3 with Spain at the Metropolitano Stadium rather than won 3-2. The reaction would not have been kind because Tuchel has been here before.

The head coach wanted to push one particular comparison from the World Cup over the summer. “It was Mexico reloaded,” he said, with a nod towards the 3-2 last-16 win at the Azteca Stadium and it fitted like a glove – down to the detail of Jarell Quansah and red cards.

Against Mexico, the defender was sent off for a late tackle in the 54th minute with England 2-1 up. Against Spain, he contributed to Elliot Anderson being sent off in the 63rd minute with England 3-0 up. Quansah had his pocket picked by Lamine Yamal and Anderson’s attempt to chase back and rectify the situation ended with him fouling the winger.

It was not only a red card but a penalty; the prompt for Spain to launch a furious and hitherto unadvertised fightback. It had the stand that housed the press box shaking. Structural integrity was very much a theme.

As in Mexico, Tuchel made defensive changes. This time, it was Myles Lewis-Skelly for Harry Kane; Djed Spence for Anthony Gordon. Tuchel also withdrew Jude Bellingham, who went off shaking his head. It was easy to understand his frustration. He was excellent. Tuchel had removed his two prime attackers. He also put Dan Burn on towards the end, albeit this time not as part of a back five. England stayed in a 4-4-1 formation, with Quansah moving from central defence to right-back. As in Mexico, the 10-man low block resisted.

As much as Tuchel disagreed, this felt like Argentina reloaded as well. “No, not at all,” he said, when the World Cup semi-final defeat was raised. “Because of one man down. We would not have been in this situation if it was 11 against 11.”

The parallels, nevertheless, were there. Tuchel made defensive substitutions at 1-0 up against Argentina; it was a back five on that occasion. As against Spain, his team could not get out and they faced a flurry of chances. There were other factors in play at the World Cup, chief among them the high levels of fatigue within the squad. England could not hold out, conceding two late goals to exit and bring down a wave of criticism on Tuchel.

The score is the ultimate takeaway. It can skew analysis. Had Trafford not got back up after parrying a shot from the Spain substitute Fermín López to brilliantly repel Aymeric Laporte’s follow‑up, England would have gone from enjoying a fabulous result to stewing over an opportunity missed. The stakes were nowhere near as high as at the World Cup, but they would have gone from finishing top of their Nations League group to advancing into the quarter-finals as an unseeded second-place team.

In terms of Tuchel’s approach to the closing stages of a big game, what changed?

The truth for England lay in the opening 63 minutes. This was where the evidence of a decisive shift could be found, the reasons for the swell of optimism. England have never played better under Tuchel – and this was against the team to beat; the world and European champions. On their turf.

Spain were without the injured Rodri and Dani Olmo, and Luis de la Fuente strangely decided to use Pedri only as a substitute, but their lineup still shimmered with menace; Lamine Yamal was frightening. Yet before their penalty, converted by Mikel Oyarzabal, they did not have a shot on target. Or a real chance.

What stood out from the first whistle was England’s front‑foot intent; the bravery on the ball. They believed they would win and there was a fearlessness about them. They made forward moves on the half turn. There was a slickness about their combinations.

Spain have never suffered like this under De la Fuente and it was everything Tuchel had dreamed of when he started to plot a new version of his team after the World Cup; a more fluid game model, a response to the Argentina defeat.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Tuchel loved England’s buildup play, which included some of Trafford’s passing. He loved the high press; the aggression in the duels; the threat on set pieces. He said he loved the low-block defending too. Ben White was excellent at right-back and there was a coming-of-age performance from Lewis Hall at left-back, but it felt wrong to single out individuals.

“We didn’t stop and I think we are ready to go [like this] for 90 minutes,” Tuchel said. “It was a complete performance and we will not look back now. Go forward and stay hungry. We will not go back on this way of playing that we find ourselves since the World Cup.”

Ezri Konsa, who headed in the second goal from a Declan Rice corner, said England “would have scored two more” if they had kept 11 men on the pitch. “You saw until the red card how much quality we had,” he said.

“We dominated the game. The instruction was to keep going at them. Don’t stop. To keep our foot on the pedal. Argentina was different; different circumstances.”

Tuchel was asked about the journey from the heartbreak of Argentina to this point; the end of a stirring Nations League group campaign, including the 7-0 win against Croatia in Rijeka. It has not all been super exciting; the 2-1 Wembley win against Croatia last Thursday, for example, was a grind. Was he always confident of a successful reboot?

“It took me a while to digest [the World Cup] and see the way forward,” he said. “How we can help and adjust and improve? We had reviews and so on but the clarity came in the first Nations League camp [in September and October] with the players.

“The first week was not so easy. Some players were still upset from the World Cup. Some were new in the team. Some had digested it, some had not. But it was important to have this process together and everyone committed to wanting to improve in certain aspects of the game.

“We had the energy right to take the next steps and from there we went. Full credit to the players, how they buy in. It’s amazing that it came together like this now.”

#879. How Frank can restore reputation and save Crystal Palace

Crystal Palace are Thomas Frank's third London club after previous spells with Brentford and Tottenham

"When the time is right I will look forward to my return as a manager, ready to embrace the job with great energy and dedication," said Thomas Frank in June.

That time is now after the Dane was confirmed as the new manager of Crystal Palace, who are two points and a goal difference deficit away from safety at the bottom of the Premier League.

Former boss Pierre Sage was sacked last week after just 16 league and cup games.

The role offers Frank an opportunity to rebuild his reputation after he was sacked by Tottenham in February after eight months.

Frank described it as "an honour" to be "in charge of this fantastic football club" as Palace announced his arrival on a deal running to June 2029.

"Crystal Palace is an iconic club in England and in the Premier League," Frank told Palace's website.

"I will do everything I possibly can to help and support the players and everyone around the place, and I'm really looking forward to meeting them."

Palace chairman Steve Parish said Frank was the "perfect fit for our club".

But how big is the challenge at Selhurst Park that awaits the man who made his name at Brentford?

"It's going to be a bit of a shock for Thomas Frank," former West Ham and England goalkeeper Rob Green tells BBC Sport.

"He had his success at Brentford - a very well-run club where players are brought in with a lot of thinking and planning to take over the players they sell for profit.

"They lose players and then have a mad scramble to get players in. They have a team that has been decimated by sales and not replaced by the same quality.

"Thomas Frank needs to find something within that team that builds and garners the belief that means that they can compete in the Premier League, because it feels a long way short of that right now."

Will Frank prove the right fit for Palace and haul the Eagles out of the relegation zone?

Since getting the sack at Tottenham after 26 league games last season, Frank has been out of management longer than he was in charge of Spurs.

In the summer he released a statement in which he said "there have been conversations and opportunities" to return to management, but that he had "decided not to rush into the next role".

Frank's name was heavily linked with Palace before they went for a head coach with no Premier League experience to replace Oliver Glasner - the man who delivered an FA Cup, a Conference League title and the Community Shield before moving to Nottingham Forest.

"Palace had one of the best managers they have had, if not forever, silverware coming across the doorstep. Look at what they achieved last season and instead of building on that, they dismantled a team," said former Tottenham and England goalkeeper Paul Robinson.

Frank once described managing as being on a "hamster wheel" and a "crazy circus"., external

Palace confirmed his coaching staff will include current assistant manager Paddy McCarthy and goalkeeping coach Andy Quy, who previously worked with him at Brentford.

Justin Cochrane, who is part of Thomas Tuchel's England staff, is set to join.

Palace are also in the process of approaching Chelsea set-piece coach Bernardo Cueva, who would join as assistant first-team coach.

It is understood Frank would like to take Andreas Georgson from Tottenham, though the north London club are determined to keep the Swede.

Denmark fitness coach Chris Haslam, who worked with Frank at Tottenham, is another potential member of Palace's new coaching set-up.

A trip to Coventry City awaits Palace on Saturday.

So why does Frank feel now is the right moment to return to management at a club propping up the table?

Frank, who was part of BBC Sport's World Cup punditry team during the summer, will be coming into the job refreshed and with renewed energy and enthusiasm following several months out of the game.

Between his appointment as Brentford boss in October 2018 and the sack at Tottenham earlier this year, he managed without a break for seven years and four months.

Spending the past few months away from Premier League pressure has allowed Frank, in his own words, to "study, observe and learn from other leaders both within sport and beyond".

Will his positivity and passion rub off on a Palace team who have lost seven times in 10 top-flight matches?

Would Thomas Frank be a good fit for Crystal Palace?

Frank, who places a major emphasis on set-piece organisation, will have to hit the ground running at Palace, who have lost their past four league games.

They have conceded more goals than anyone else in the Premier League (24) and have scored only 10 themselves.

"If you want someone to go in and restore some stability and defensive solidity while improving the set-piece element of the team, then Thomas Frank is the perfect man for the job," Times football writer Tom Allnutt told BBC Radio 5 Live's Football Daily podcast.

With the Premier League season just 10 games old, Frank certainly has time to turn it around and will have targets in mind when the transfer window opens in January.

Palace sold France centre-back Maxence Lacroix to Chelsea for Â£52m and Colombia right-back Daniel Munoz to Nottingham Forest for Â£22m during the summer transfer window.

Allnutt added: "We know they have sold so many good players and so far I don't think they have really replaced them adequately."

Another challenge for Frank is getting midfielder Adam Wharton, who has not played for England since March, back to something like his best form.

These are all challenges the new manager will relish.

After his bruising experience at Tottenham - having established Brentford in the Premier League - Frank has decided to climb back on the hamster wheel with Palace.

"Crystal Palace and Thomas Frank feels like a very good fit," added Robinson.

Crystal Palace fan calls Thomas Frank 'the perfect hire'

Thomas Frank has a lot of work to do as Crystal Palace have undoubtedly been the worst team in the Premier League so far this season, ranking bottom not just in points (seven) but also goal difference (-14) and expected goal difference (-8.1).

It's the defence where Frank will have to focus most of his attention. Not only have Palace conceded the most goals (24) but they've also faced the most shots (189) and have the worst expected goals against (xGA) figure in the league (21.9).

Their attack has actually not been too bad. While only Hull have taken fewer shots, the Eagles have created really good chances and have perhaps been unlucky not to score a few more goals given the opportunities they've had.

There is also one significant factor in Frank's favour. Although Palace may be bottom of the Premier League, they are certainly not cut adrift as they sit just two points from safety.

The side propping up the table at this stage have had an average of just three points in the past 10 seasons, but for as bad as they've been, Palace have seven - the most the bottom side have had after 10 games for 24 years.

#878. Are Scotland still too reliant on 'old guard'?

Scotland slump to 4-0 defeat in Switzerland

As Zeki Amdouni arrowed in second-string Switzerland's fabulous fourth goal, the body language of dejected Scotland duo Andy Robertson and Ryan Christie was telling.

The captain's record-breaking 103rd cap played out in cruel fashion. Suited and booted for the occasion, with commemorative boots and a personalised armband, there was no cause for celebration as Robertson was, yet again, wheeled out afterwards to make sense of the 4-0 scudding in St Gallen.

So too were John McGinn and Kieran Tierney. Billy Gilmour, who has also surpassed the half-century caps landmark, also did a bit of talking. Substitute Christie was spared this time.

After a result of this kind, rounding up a humdrum maiden campaign for manager Sebastien Pocognoli, it's necessary for the experienced heads to front-up.

When he named his first squad, so much kudos was thrown the Belgian's way for breaking away from the norm and bleeding in the stars of tomorrow.

But such young and bright lights were only allowed to shine on the bench, at best, as Pocognoli turned to the tried and tested.

As former Scotland international Leanne Crichton said on BBC Scotland's Sportscene: "There's a reliance still, clearly, on that key core of Scotland players.

"And, when you listen to it post-match, they sound dejected, they don't sound that confident about what is going on. It is a difficult place to be."

Pocognoli's abject Scotland suffer 4-0 Nations League defeat in Switzerland

St Gallen was a mighty troubling place for the Scots on Monday night.

The calm, picturesque city was invaded by coral shirt and kilt-clad Scotsmen from Sunday, but they - and their heroes on the pitch - couldn't wait to get out of the place after a poor showing at the Sitterstadion.

A narrow half-time deficit turned into a drubbing on the final whistle, at which the Scots remained goalless despite a handful of hopeful situations.

McGinn, the scorer of Scotland's past three goals, directed a weak header goalbound before the break, while Scott McTominay - nearly one year on from his Hampden heroics against Denmark - missed a couple of glaring opportunities.

"If McTominay is not operating at his highest level for the national team, there is an impact on results," Crichton said.

"If McGinn doesn't produce the goods on an evening, we're in trouble.

"If Gilmour and Ferguson in the middle of the pitch [don't perform], if Christie doesn't come on with an impact, we are [too reliant].

"And that's where you need to breed a different confidence in a different group."

Kieron Bowie, who many hoped would be in from the off, came on just before the hour mark and got right in about it, as is the striker's style.

Winger Ben Gannon-Doak, dropped for Aaron Hickey, did come on after the wing-back ended up going off with an apparent hamstring injury before Kristi Montgomery was handed a debut with five minutes to go.

Wide-men Findlay Curtis and Josh McPake were left on the bench, again. Robbie Ure didn't make either matchday squad this camp.

All three natural wingers excite supporters, even if they have only been handed a matter of minutes, but Pocognoli's system does not suit them.

That said, the players insist they're invested in the project.

"We have to believe that we're going in the right direction," Robertson added after a beyond-deflating defeat.

"Of course, there's going to be humps in the road, but when I look back on Steve Clarke's opening six games - I can't remember all the results but - I don't think everyone was shouting and screaming about Steve Clarke's Scotland after the first six games.

"We're trying to get a team together and we're trying to build a good atmosphere off the pitch.

"People wanted change within the squad. We've done that change and now we need to try and integrate the squad.

"We need to get close as a squad again, integrate the young players, make them feel a part of it, make them step up - it's for us to try and help them do it."

What's the story with Pocognoli, is it now time to go?

#877. Max Dowman shines in England colours and sends another record tumbling

Midfielder’s under-21s winner eclipsed Jude Bellingham’s mark and there was other talent to admire against France

There may have been an Mbappé on the pitch – Ethan, the younger brother of Kylian, with whom he shares a near-identical gait – but by the end there was only one precocious talent on the lips of those watching England overcome France in their under-21s clash. Max Dowman had done it again, lighting up another game, this time in filthy conditions at Ashton Gate. It was fitting he had the final say in a 3-2 win. The noise that accompanied his match-winning goal? Well, beyond the palpable excitement in the stands in Bristol, that would be the sound of the teenager sending yet another record tumbling.

Which one takes your fancy? Take your pick. At 14, playing for Arsenal Under-19s, he became the Uefa Youth League’s youngest goalscorer. This time last year, after taking to the field at Slavia Prague aged 15 and 308 days, Dowman became the youngest player to feature in the Champions League. In March, six months on from his professional debut, he became the Premier League’s youngest goalscorer. He is the youngest player to earn a Premier League winner’s medal. Last month he was presented with three Guinness World Records.

In scoring his first under-21s goal, in the penultimate minute of regular time, Dowman eclipsed Jude Bellingham to become the team’s youngest scorer at 16 years and 320 days, three days after surpassing the Real Madrid midfielder’s record as the under-21s’ youngest player. Bellingham was almost four months older than Dowman when he scored his first goal for the age group, in September 2020. Bellingham made only four appearances for the under-21s, a result of being fast-tracked into the senior team, and Dowman could emulate him again, though he is expected to feature in next summer’s Under-21 European Championship in Albania and Serbia.

The common view from coaches and teammates, and something stressed by Lee Carsley, the under-21s head coach, is that it is easy to forget Dowman is six weeks shy of his 17th birthday. Against France, it was also extremely easy to overlook that this was Dowman’s first start for the under-21s, after a substitute appearance against Portugal last Friday. His first action set the tone on Monday, using his body to box off the ball then jinking up the right flank, zipping it through the legs of Dayann Methalie before skating forward and sending the Sunderland left-back juddering on to his backside.

Dowman exhibited plenty of neat touches, and a couple of effortless first-time passes, but those who have watched him develop say his work rate and willingness to do the other side of the game are among his biggest strengths.

“We look at Max and see how good he is on the ball, how attacking he is, but I thought he was outstanding off the ball,” Carsley said, presumably thinking of the moment Dowman scampered deep into his own half to intercept a stray France pass. He was not finished after scoring either. At one point he had five blue shirts haring after him as he stormed into the France half and, seconds later, his quick feet lured the opposition captain, Nathan Zézé, into a foul on the edge of the France penalty area.

Dowman is among the next wave of players pushing to step up to Thomas Tuchel’s squad, perhaps at its forefront. It is a well-trodden path and the current crop need not look too far for inspiration. Elliot Anderson and Jarell Quansah, both of whom started England’s triumph at the last under-21 Euros in Bratislava, began Sunday’s memorable victory for the seniors in Madrid. Jobe Bellingham and Josh King are the latest players to make the transition into Tuchel’s squad and more will follow.

Jack Hinshelwood and Trey Nyoni, of Brighton and Liverpool respectively, impressed at the base of midfield and the 19-year-old Mikey Moore, another to score on his first start for the under-21s, shone down the left flank, opening the scoring. The Everton midfielder Harrison Armstrong entered as a substitute and supplied Dowman’s winner, and Armstrong’s clubmate Tyrique George also showed promise after replacing Moore. Archie Gray captained the under-21s against Portugal but did not feature on Monday, with Carsley revealing he has spoken to the Tottenham midfielder about Scotland wanting him to switch allegiance. “I just said to him: ‘Keep me in the picture, if it’s something that you were thinking of,’” Carsley said. “I think Archie is very connected to our pathway.”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

England’s budding talent is not confined to the under-21s. Carsley took a closer look at Brian Madjo, the imposing 17-year-old striker who scored on his Aston Villa debut in the Super Cup in August, the Manchester United defender Ayden Heaven and the West Brom forward Jimmy-Jay Morgan, who signed from Chelsea in the summer, before his squad departed for Bristol last week, the trio joining the under-21s for four days of training at St George’s Park.

Dowman, after two under-21 appearances comprising a little more than 120 minutes, is putting the squeeze on. “Max is doing something special for his age and he is pushing people a lot older than him,” said Moore, who is on loan from Tottenham at Köln and hopes to face his idol Harry Kane and Bayern Munich on Friday. “He’s a top kid. You kind of forget how old he is. My little brother is 17 and he [Dowman] feels older to me than my little brother … He has been top and everywhere he goes, he just takes that next step.”

#876. When is the Nations League quarter-final draw?

England are a seeded side for the Nations League quarter-finals after topping their group

The draw for the final eight teams in the 2026-27 Nations League will be on Friday, 20 November at 11:00 GMT.

It will take place at Uefa's headquarters in Nyon, Switzerland and be broadcast on Uefa TV.

England are the only home nation to have made it to the quarter-final stage, however Northern Ireland's draw against Hungary saw them top Group B2 and secure promotion to League A in the 2028-29 tournament.

Scotland will remain in League B following their third-place finish in Group B1, and Wales face a League A/B relegation play-off in March after being consigned to last place in Group A4.

The Republic of Ireland finished second in Group B3 and so will take part in a League A/B promotion play-off in March.

The winners of groups A1-A4 are seeded for the draw, playing the runners-up of other groups in League A.

England have sealed their place in the last eight as Group A3 winners and could face:

They cannot face A3 runners-up Spain as teams must be drawn against sides from other groups.

The quarter-finals will be played over two legs during the international break between 25-30 March.

Seeded teams get to play the second leg of their quarter-final at home.

Nations that reach the semi-finals can bid those penultimate matches as well as the final.

The remaining dates for the Nations League are:

Semi-finals, third-place play-off and final: 9-13 June

#875. Danny Kelly obituary

Ebullient journalist, magazine editor and broadcaster whose passion for music and football shone through all his work

Danny Kelly, who has died aged 69, influenced music journalism and sports broadcasting for more than four decades. Humour, enthusiasm and encyclopedic knowledge were the hallmarks of his work as a writer and editor at the New Musical Express (NME) and Q magazine, and throughout his online, TV and audio career, most prominently around his passion for football.

In 1997 Kelly helped set up Football 365, one of the earliest football websites, and still one of the most popular in the UK. He hosted radio shows on BBC 5 Live, TalkSport, BT Sport and Times Radio, as well as many podcasts including The View from the Lane, about the team he had supported since childhood, Tottenham Hotspur.

Kelly’s deputy at the NME, Stuart Maconie, described how he championed “the best of everything … roots, rock, reggae, the Smiths, Tamla Motown, the Clash, T.Rex, prog”. His close friend Danny Baker, his regular co-host since 1992, said that they shared “music, football, life … an absurd private universe of turmoil” together and turned to humour “to forge another path for football punditry, based in hoopla, voodoo and toasters”.

Kelly’s much-shared 2008 commentary of an Arsenal and Spurs match, alongside the retired footballer Stan Collymore, exemplified his relatable passion: “I love football, Stan! I love it!” he shouted when Spurs equalised, adding, seconds later, “How unprofessional.” Collymore described how Kelly brought him to TalkSport after he struggled with chronic mental health issues; Kelly gave many others support during their own physical and psychological struggles.

Born in London, into a family that had recently emigrated from County Carlow in Ireland to Islington, Danny was the oldest of the six children of Josie (nee Martin), a school dinner lady, and Andy, a railway worker.

Despite growing up “literally in the shadow of Highbury Stadium”, and in a family of Arsenal supporters, Danny supported their near-rivals. Speaking to FourFourTwo magazine in 2006, he said that Spurs represented “the true spirit of rock’n’roll”.

A pupil at Sacred Heart primary school in Holloway and later at St Aloysius’ College in Highgate, Kelly loved history (“but I don’t suppose anyone really cares about my opinions about the Anglo-Prussian agreements of the 17th century,” he told the New York Times’ sports website The Athletic in 2022).

In a 2020 interview with the Behind the Lines podcast, he described himself as “teenage music fanatic”, calling the NME in the mid-1970s his “bible”.

After failing to complete law and combined arts studies at Leicester University through “lack of effort, and punk rock”, he worked at British Rail on the complaints counter and as a station announcer. As a shop steward with the Transport Salaried Staffs’ Association, he wrote about music in the union magazine. A copy picked up by the NME jazz critic Richard Cook at a TUC conference in 1983 led to freelance work for Kelly, who then returned to college to pursue media studies at the Polytechnic of Central London (now the University of Westminster).

His writing was ebullient and vivid: Marvin Gaye possessed “a combination of gifts seldom stuffed into one body, one psyche”; the Smiths made “a Catherine wheel of inspired language” against “shifting, sometimes unnervingly evocative and beautiful guitar music”. Joining the NME in 1985 as a writer, he became deputy editor in 1987 and editor in 1990, before taking over Q in 1992.

There, he commanded audiences in the office and at after-work pub sessions regaling his stories of meeting musicians, and presented serious cover stars with characteristic irreverence: Sting, formerly of the Police, in handcuffs; Kate Bush under the headline “Booze, fags, blokes and me”.

In 1995, he launched Total Sport magazine, which ran for four years, and from 1997 to 1998 presented the late-night Channel 4 sports and entertainment show Under the Moon. Simultaneously, he ran editorial operations for Football 365, which became popular during the 1998 World Cup.

His subsequent radio career was prolific and popular. On TalkSport’s This Sporting Life, his interviewees included Virginia Wade, Frank Bruno and Eric Bristow. Trans Euro Express combined his love of European football and music, while his expertise in other sports, including cycling and American football, was in regular demand.

A year-long marriage ended in 1998; in 2005, the literary journalist and editor Alex Clark became his partner. He married her, wearing shoes from a range by his favourite rapper, MF Doom, in 2021. They moved to Kilkenny in 2018 to be near his mother, who had returned to Ireland.

Kelly broadcast remotely throughout the pandemic, up until his diagnosis with oesophageal cancer in March. He posted a diary of his treatment, the Kelly Cancer Kronikles, to his 106,000 followers on X until August, its title referencing one of his literary heroes, the fictional schoolboy Nigel Molesworth.

“I hope that what I’ve done over the years is to be honest and open about football, life, culture, everything else,” he said to the Athletic, and added the only two pieces of advice he ever gave to aspiring broadcasters. “Be a version of yourself, but add an extra 15% of personality. And don’t be shit. Try not to be shit and you’ll be OK.”

Alex, his mother, Josie, and his siblings, Margaret, Michael, Andrew, Joanna and John, survive him.

Daniel John Kelly, journalist and broadcaster, born 22 December 1956; died 10 November 2026
