#837. Will Infantino feel he's already won as Fifa challengers are revealed?

Gianni Infantino has been president of Fifa since 2016 and is standing for re-election for a third time

Uefa has finally identified a candidate to take on Gianni Infantino in next year's Fifa presidential election.

Less than 48 hours before Wednesday night's deadline, European football's governing body announced that French Football Federation (FFF) president Philippe Diallo had received the unanimous support of its executive committee.

A late and surprise choice, Diallo said, "I think I have the experience, the convictions and the values which offer a credible alternative...I'm entering this campaign not just to provide a different voice, but to win."

But he is not the Frenchman some believe Uefa really wanted, as it tries to remove Infantino in the wake of his failed plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

Senior figures in European football had hoped to persuade Arsene Wenger - Fifa's head of global development - to stand against his own boss. Some felt that only he possessed the credibility to pose a serious threat to Infantino's plans for a fourth term.

But after the former Arsenal manager chose not to proceed, Uefa had no choice but to seek an alternative.

So just how credible a challenger is Diallo? Does Infantino's position appear unassailable? And how could he still be stopped from winning another term?

Wenger decides not to challenge Fifa chief Infantino

Politicians, private jets and power - the life of a Fifa president

An administrator who has worked in French football since 1992 and became FFF president in 2023, Diallo is not a household name. But he has already shown he is prepared to stand up to Infantino.

In September, Diallo claimed he had "seriously damaged the image and unity of football", and said "trust has been broken" over the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) sell-off plot.

According to Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister, Diallo is a "candidate who can instigate real, meaningful and lasting reform" within the governing body.

"We've always made it very clear that our objectives and motivations are driving culture change. That means wide-ranging, systemic reform of football governance rather than simply the replacement of an individual leader," McAllister told BBC Sport.

"I've known Philippe since we were both elected to Uefa's executive committee, and he's an intelligent, honest, sharp-minded football person with an impressive experience of governance in one of the world's football power-houses. Most importantly, he is a person of integrity... Philippe is a fantastic advocate for the change agenda that football needs, and I know his campaign will reflect that."

Infantino remains the favourite to win a majority of the 211 votes, and is thought to have the support of most of Africa (54 members), Asia (47) and South America (10).

However, Uefa hopes that Diallo - whose father was a Senegalese boxing champion who represented France in the 1960 Olympics - could enjoy support in parts of Africa and beyond. He claims he already has the backing of countries beyond Europe.

Laura McAllister is a former captain of the Wales women's football team

While most of Europe's national associations are expected to vote for Diallo, it is clear that he was not Uefa's first choice. "I wasn't initially a candidate, but the insistence of my European colleagues led me to accept the offer", he admitted.

Uefa only approached Diallo about standing in the past week, and senior officials at some European national associations have also told BBC Sport they are frustrated with the failure to find a higher-profile candidate sooner.

Speaking anonymously, one said they only learned about Diallo's potential candidacy on Sunday, and that while they were supportive of him, "it would have been helpful if we'd had someone much earlier" and "a lot of eggs were put in the Wenger basket."

They also made the point that Diallo was yet to publish a manifesto, and questioned whether he could really win.

Another expressed similar sentiments, saying Diallo was a good man, but "not seen as a heavyweight". They claimed that Uefa had "lost the momentum. The process hasn't been great. I really hope they've got a rabbit to pull out of the hat."

McAllister is optimistic: "I have no doubt whatsoever that we will collectively mount a powerful campaign with the objective of winning the election next March". she said.

"The really critical period comes next, once candidate nominations close and eligibility checks are complete."

Despite high-profile critics like Germany manager Jurgen Klopp - who this week said "the opinion is unanimous that a change would make sense" - Infantino does appear to be in a position of strength.

As recently as August it all seemed very different. Fifa's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour strongly criticised Infantino, while a senior adviser, Carlos Cordeiro, resigned. The heads of three confederations - Uefa, the Asian Football Confederation and Concacaf, which runs the game in North and Central America - then signed a letter accusing the Fifa president of breaking trust "through deception".

Amid an increasingly acrimonious civil war, Infantino seemed vulnerable. But the revolt against him then suffered a series of setbacks.

First, Fifa's executives backed Infantino at a crunch meeting in Rabat. Uefa then called off a threatened boycott of Fifa competitions, while potential rivals such as Concacaf chief Victor Montagliani decided not to stand. Aleksander Ceferin chose to stay for a fourth term as Uefa president rather than challenge Infantino directly.

Meanwhile, Infantino's position as the incumbent enabled him to embark on what has appeared to be a world tour, shoring up support. His chances of re-election received another major boost when he proposed to increase the amount of money handed out by Fifa for football development across the world by Â£2.6 billion.

Sheikh Salman, the head of the Asian Football Confederation, then performed a U-turn, endorsing Infantino, who soon after told the BBC he had the backing of the "vast, vast majority" of world football.

"I'm a professor of politics so I never assume that there's a runaway favourite to win any election", insists McAllister.

"There are plenty of twists and turns to come in this story between now and the election at Fifa's Congress next year.

"This is about structural change and a commitment to modernising the way in which football is governed so it benefits all who play and watch...that imperative will remain and we will hold the new president accountable for much-needed change."

"The current weaknesses of global football governance have been brutally exposed of late. This has helped coalesce and unite opposition to Gianni Infantino, but also to articulate the widely-held demands that things must change."

So with just four months until the presidential election, where could Infantino still run into difficulties?

Litigation is arguably the most obvious. As part of its wider plan to remove Infantino, Uefa has filed court documents in the US, which includes a potential criminal complaint against him in Switzerland for alleged financial mismanagement.

The legal action has not yet appeared to trouble him. But some senior figures in the European game remain hopeful it could still force Fifa to hand over evidence related to FFE that could prove damaging to Infantino's re-election prospects.

There is pressure from elsewhere in football. Fifa has already agreed to make "key documents" relating to the FFE plan available to members of its council. Infantino's critics believe this disclosure may reveal details that could increase the pressure on him before the election. Last month, the Norwegian Football Federation also submitted a three-part ethics complaint to Fifa regarding the awarding of a Peace Prize to US President Donald Trump, the Folarin Balogun case at the World Cup, and the FFE plot.

The Democrats' victory in the US midterm elections means scrutiny from beyond the sport too. Earlier this year, Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee launched an inquiry into Infantino's ties with Trump. In September, a spokeswoman said FIfa's co-operation with the investigation had been "woefully inadequate." But armed with extra powers, they could now force him to hand over relevant documents or give evidence.

Recent months have also seen a series of potentially damaging stories emerge in the media about various aspects of Infantino's leadership. So far they seem to have done little harm to his re-election chances, with Fifa claiming "it is evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine [him]". But the scrutiny is likely to continue.

Could Infantino even be ruled ineligible to stand? According to Portuguese lawyer Miguel Maduro - a former head of Fifa's governance committee - Infantino should not be allowed to be a candidate in the election as Fifa rules limit presidents to three terms. In 2022, Fifa's Council agreed that his first period in office - between 2016 and 2019 - should not count as he was effectively completing the remainder of Blatter's term after his resignation. But as Maduro has said, a national association or confederation would need to challenge this decision at the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS).

Japan Football Association honorary president, Kozo Tashima, has announced his intention to stand, along with former Tottenham Hotspur defender Ramon Vega. But with uncertainty over how much support either man will have, it seems Diallo is the challenger most likely to test the strength of Infantino's supporter base. There is a danger that the vote against Infantino is split.

It has not gone unnoticed at Fifa that as recently as March, Diallo was quoted congratulating Infantino when the Fifa president visited Paris, external to highlight a mini-pitch programme and the need for more football infrastructure globally.

A lot has changed since then, however. And now the Frenchman has been tasked with finding a way of unseating Infantino, and becoming just the 10th Fifa president in its history.

#836. Nick Cannon, Moms of His 12 Kids Reveal Dynamic in Raising the Cannons

Nick Cannon—dad to twins Moroccan and Monroe with Mariah Carey and 10 children with five women—unveiled his life as a father of 12 on his new Netflix show.

Nick Cannon's family is experiencing growing pains.

The Drumline star, who is dad to 12 children, is letting fans inside his life as the head of a blended family through his upcoming docuseries Raising the Cannons.

"I have a relationship with six women and 12 children," Cannon explained in the trailer for the Netflix show, debuting Dec. 18. "This is a world that I created, and I have to deal with everything that comes with it."

And Cannon—who first became a dad after welcoming twins Moroccan and Monroe, 15, with ex Mariah Carey—has learned co-parenting can be difficult given the complex rapport between him and his partners (He’s also dad to Golden Sagon, 9, Powerful Queen, 5 and Rise Messiah, 4, with Brittany Bell, twins Zion Mixolydian and Zillion Heir, 5, and Beautiful Zeppelin, 4, with Abby De La Rosa, Halo Marie, 3, and as well as a late son, Zen, with Alyssa Scott, Legendary Love, 4, with Bre Tiesi and Onyx Ice, 4, with LaNisha Cole.)

As such, the Wild 'n Out creator—who according to Netflix is romantically involved with De La Rosa, Scott and Tiesi—explained, "I want my children to have relationships with one another. One day we all would be able to get along."

Yet Cole expressed acting as one big happy family is a performance she's not willing to put on for the cameras.

"I don't need to create this false narrative," the photographer said in confessional, "like we're one big happy family when we're not."

Meanwhile, De La Rosa had her own take on her partner's role in creating challenges between the women in his life. In her words narrating the trailer offscreen, "Nick formulates these worlds as if we're so separate. Everyone thinks it's competition. No, it's our reality."

For her part, Tiesi, who also stars on Selling Sunset, objected to the notion that she and her son had to fight for Cannon's attention, stating to cameras, "I am not in competition," while also appearing to tell Cannon on the phone the other matriarchs in their circle "broke, pathetic losers."

As for how the comedian's kids feel about their unique family dynamic? Both Moroccan and Monroe chimed in with concerns for their father, who admitted his ego sabotaged his six-year marriage with their mom, Carey, which ended in 2014.

"If you didn't have all these kids," Monroe told Cannon, "you would have been back together," referring to the Grammy winner. In turn, her twin brother suggested in their joint confessional that their dad's lifestyle was not "sustainable in any way."

Need a bird's-eye view of Cannon's expansive family tree? Keep reading...

Children No. 1 and 2: Moroccan Cannon and Monroe Cannon

Mariah Carey gave birth to her and Nick's twins on April 30, 2011. The two announced their split in 2015 after six years of marriage and finalized their divorce a year later.

Beauty queen Brittany Bell gave birth to her and Nick's first child together, a boy, on Feb. 21, 2017.

Brittany and Nick welcomed their second baby together, a girl, in December 2020.

DJ Abby De La Rosa gave birth to her and Nick's twin boys on June 14, 2021.

Model Alyssa Scott welcomed a baby boy with Nick on June 23, 2021.

However, just five months after the arrival of their son, Nick shared the devastating news that Zen had passed away from brain cancer. "Alyssa was just the strongest woman I have ever seen," he said on the Dec. 7 episode of The Nick Cannon Show. "Never had an argument, never was angry. She was emotional when she needed to be but was always the best mom and continues to be the best mom possible. So I've got to say thank you to my entire family but specifically to Alyssa."

"You never know what someone is going through," he added. "Hug your family. Kiss somebody. Tell them you love them."

Model Bre Tiesi welcomed her first child with Nick on June 28, 2022. The baby boy weighed 8 pounds and 10 ounces at birth.

"I did it. An all natural unmedicated home birth," Bre shared in a July 2022 Instagram post. "This was the most humbling / limit pushing yet awakening and completely empowering experience. I can't thank my team enough for delivering my son safely."

Nick and model LaNisha Cole welcomed a daughter on Sept. 14, 2022.

Brittany gave birth to her third child with Nick on Sept. 23, 2022.

#835. London City's Goodwin gets first England call-up

Izzy Goodwin has scored three goals in five WSL appearances for London City

London City Lionesses forward Izzy Goodwin has been named in the England squad for the first time for the World Cup qualifying play-off against Ukraine.

The 23-year-old has been in great form this month and scored in front of England manager Sarina Wiegman at Emirates Stadium on Sunday in a 1-1 draw with Arsenal.

"We have always seen her as a huge talent with potential," Wiegman told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"I think London City are developing really well in the games they have showed. She is tall and can head a ball attacking-wise, but also defending.

"She is really quick with her feet and can score goals. I really want to see her in our environment, what she can bring and how close she is to the level that we expect."

There is also a first call-up for goalkeeper Katie Cox, on loan at Nottingham Forest from Chelsea, while Manchester United midfielder Ella Toone returns.

Manchester City duo Niamh Charles and Alex Greenwood, who is injured, are among those to miss out.

The Lionesses play Ukraine in Spain on 1 December before hosting them at Wembley on 5 December. The winner qualifies for next year's Women's World Cup.

"We know what's at stake in these games and our focus is on producing two strong performances to secure our place at the World Cup," said Wiegman.

"We have worked hard to put ourselves in this position and now we have to finish the job.

"Ukraine will provide a challenge and we will prepare with the same focus and determination that we always do."

Chelsea defender Lucy Bronze could make her 150th appearance at Wembley in the second leg.

England travel to Pinatar, Spain a few days before the first leg and opted not to play a friendly match during this extended international break.

"The first part of the block we are [at St George's Park]. We have training sessions and a period of time where we can do some tactical stuff," added Wiegman.

"We also selected more players so that helps us create situations where we can train things and everyone is important. I'm really excited to get ready for these games."

Sarina Wiegman led England to victory at Euro 2022 and Euro 2025

Wiegman was speaking to media at St George's Park for the first time since signing a new contract that will run until the end of Euro 2029.

It means she could oversee England's fortunes at next year's World Cup if they beat Ukraine, as well as heading up a Team GB squad at the 2028 Olympic Games.

Asked why she wanted to extend her stay, Wiegman told BBC Radio 5 Live: "Well, first of all the FA is happy with me and I'm really happy with them.

"I'm really grateful for that environment. That is one [reason]. Secondly, I still feel a great connection with staff and players, and of course the country!

"Then we have the challenges ahead. The major tournaments always motivate me. You don't get many moments with the team because it's not like it is at a club.

"In a tournament, you have those moments where you are really together, you can get somewhere with the group and that really excites me.

"Yes, the Olympics would be really great. Next year it's the World Cup, then it's the Olympics, then it's the Euros â that journey ahead really excites me."

Wiegman's contract renewal was kept under wraps and it came as a surprise following their two-legged victory over Greece in October.

The Dutchwoman, who has guided England to successive European titles, said conversations had been ongoing for a while but she had not planned ahead.

"When I signed that first contract in 2020 to join in 2021, it was a four-year contract and I thought, 'ok, this is a long contract, it would be really great if things go well'.

"We all got so excited so I signed another contract until 2027 and now I have until 2029. That is eight years. I never expected that. I also never planned so far ahead.

"I want to feel that I can contribute to the environment and the development of things. I also want that from the other party. You want it to fit and for it to work.

"That decision came over time. At one point you think: 'Yeah, I'm getting really excited again.' That is what you want. To feel the energy, to feel the excitement.

"I still think we have things we can improve. We know the game is improving so quickly so we have to adapt all the time. When you stand still, you are lost."

Wiegman is also determined to improve as a coach and has enjoyed overseeing the development of younger talent as the Lionesses transition.

"It starts with me and about how I am going to develop. I keep learning things about myself too. You need to know yourself really well to do this job," she added.

"The staff and the players will always challenge me in the right ways. It goes back and forth. That is what I want. I really want to improve myself all the time."

#833. UK Privy Council overrules Trinidad and Tobago gay sex law

A London court has overturned a Trinidad and Tobago law criminalizing consensual sexual relations between male same-sex couples. As a result of the colonial legacy, it is the independent country's last court of appeal.

A man from Trinidad and Tobago has won a legal appeal lasting almost a decade in the last court of appeal available to him — the judicial committee of the Privy Council in former colonial power Britain.

Jason Jones, a gay man born in Trinidad and Tobago, had challenged the Caribbean nation's Sexual Offences Act outlawing consensusal sex between adult males, saying that it breached his fundamental rights under the country's constitution.

He initially won his case at Trinidad and Tobago's High Court, but the government and religious organizations managed to partially overturn the ruling once more, prompting Jones to the take the case to the island nation's highest appellate authority — the Privy Council in  the UK.

"To discriminate against somebody simply because of who they choose to love is simply ridiculous," Jones told the Associated Press after Tuesday's judgment was rendered.

The Privy Council in London is the final court of appeal for some Commonwealth countries including Trinidad and Tobago, although that issue was already contentious in some circles prior to Tuesday's ruling.

A panel of five judges unanimously allowed Jones' appeal, dismissing a counter-appeal from the Caribbean country's Attorney General.

It found that two sections of the country's Sexual Offenses Act 1986, criminalizing "buggery" and "serious indecency" respectively among same-sex couples, violated Jones' fundamental rights to private and family life set out in the 1976 constitution.

The court wrote in its ruling that "the rights and interests of Mr Jones which are at stake involve a particularly important facet of his existence and identity since the ability to form an intimate and loving relationship with another person lies at the core of the right to private and family life."

The anti-gay laws that call for up to five years in prison have not been enforced in recent history, but critics say they still send an intimidating message.

Judge Philip Sales said as he announced the ruling that "the current understanding of the fundamental individual right to respect for private and family life is that it protects such a core part of human identity as one's sexual orientation."

Sales added that "laws which seek to criminalize such activities cannot be justified."

Trinidadian authorities argued that because the 1986 laws were passed with a super-majority and constituted criminal penalties that dated back to colonial times, prior to the constitution, they could be considered "existing law" and override the individual constitutional rights in certain circumstances.

But the Privy Council judges found that the so-called "proviso" for this special status — "unless the Act is shown not to be reasonably justifiable in a society that has proper respect for the rights and freedoms of the individual" — had not been met.

One of Jones' lawyers, Anand Ramlogan, is a former attorney general of Trinidad and Tobago and argued against this position earlier in the case.

"Constitutional rights exist precisely because majorities are not always right," Ramlogan said. "They ensure that the dignity and equality of every citizen are not left to the changing tides of public opinion."

Jason Jones is a 61-year-old born in Trinidad and Tobago.

Openly gay since the age of 16, he said he fled the country in 1996 because of homophobic violence and discrimination.

Speaking to the Associated Press on Tuesday after what he termed a "stunning victory," he said he would describe himself as a "very angry gay man," whose anger had helped him persist in his legal appeal for so many years.

"Society has treated me worse than a criminal," he said. "There is a real sense of vindication with this judgment. Finally, the courts are seeing that they need to step up because our politicians are so toothless."

He said he became inspired to speak out after losing friends to HIV/AIDS and after meeting American singer-songwriter Nina Simone when she toured the island nation for three weeks in 1984, when he was 19.

"Nina was the one who said, 'Jason, get off this rock and go see the world,'" he said, calling it a defining and life-changing experience.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trinidad and Tobago's government, the country's Council of Evangelical Churches and its largest Hindu organization, Sanatan Dharm Maha Sabha, contested the case, which has wound its way through several courts since the appeal was launched in 2017.

In 2018, Trinidad's High Court found the laws unconstitutional. But in 2025, a local appeals court partially reversed the ruling. Trinidad's Court of Appeals subsequently allowed Jones to seek a ruling from the final appeals court in England.

The case was being closely watched by activists across the Caribbean, with similar laws in place in several other countries in the region.

The Bahamas decriminalized homosexuality in 1991.

The UK repealed laws in overseas territories Anguilla, the British Virgin Islands, the Cayman Islands, Montserrat and the Turks and Caicos Islands in 2001.

Judges in Barbados, Dominica, St. Lucia and Antigua and Barbuda have also recently struck down similar laws.

But in former British colonies Grenada, Jamaica, Trinidad and Tobago and St. Vincent and the Grenadines it remains a crime.

The UK only decriminalized gay sex in 1967, more than four centuries after the so-called "buggery" laws were first introduced under King Henry VII, and more than a century after the last executions for the crime. People still faced prosecution or the threat of it for consensual adult gay sex until after World War II, with surely the most famous later-years case being that of computing and codebreaking pioneer and war hero Alan Turing.

#832. FA wants to host Nations League finals in England

England finished top of their Nations League group

England could host the Nations League finals this season after Football Association officials registered their interest.

The semi-final and finals of the competition, due to take place in June, are held in one country.

As well as England, it is understood that Spain and France have also contacted Uefa to register their interest in hosting the final four games, including the bronze medal match, which will run between 9-13 June.

The FA, it is understood, is still discussing potential venues with some doubt over whether Wembley would be available. The only publicly announced Wembley events in June are two concerts by singer Sam Fender, although these are for after the Nations League.

Since the tournament began in 2019, England have never held the finals, with Portugal, Italy, Netherlands and Germany the hosts to date.

Generally, only nations who reach the last four of the Nations League are considered to host the latter stages.

Thomas Tuchel's team will be seeded in Friday's draw for the quarter-finals following their euphoric 3-2 victory over Spain in Madrid, which secured top place in the group.

They could face Belgium, Netherlands, Denmark or Norway in March in the next round before June's finals.

If the FA's bid is successful, it will provide the governing body with an opportunity to host a mini-tournament before Euro 2028, which will be held in England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.

#831. Janine van Wyk: ‘Our rooms were empty … no mattresses, no lightbulbs and not a drop of water’

In an extract from the former South Africa captain’s book, she details less than ideal Wafcon 2006 preparations

I was just a year into my international career when we qualified for my first Wafcon, which was then called the African Women’s Championship (AWC) and was held in Nigeria in 2006. I was extremely excited but very nervous to participate in this tournament, more so when it was announced that we would be in the same group as the hosts, and would play them last in the group.

As it turned out, it would be the game that decided who finished top of the group. By then we had beaten Algeria 4-0 and Equatorial Guinea 2-0 and had to travel to Delta State to take on the hosts. I’d heard that Nigeria was the toughest country to travel to and I was about to realise why. It’s become common knowledge that South Africans and Nigerians are massive rivals on the football field but also don’t really get on off it.

We felt unwelcome from the moment we arrived and we were not the only team to experience this. Nigeria exploited all avenues to play mind games with their opposition and to make them lose focus on the matches.

We arrived early in the morning at the Murtala Muhammed international airport in Lagos and faced our first test: how to retrieve our luggage. Only one carousel was working, which meant we had to wait a long time for our bags to arrive. We had a training session planned for later in the day and were all eager to get to the hotel, settle in and prepare for our first practice.

As we stepped out the airport doors, we looked for the bus that was to take us there, but we didn’t see one anywhere. As players, we were irritable and impatient, and starting to show it. Some of us were slumped on our bags, others had taken up residence on the pavement, and we were all cranky, especially as it took over an hour before a bus arrived.

Like in Mozambique a few years before, the bus was too small. Another 21-seater and we were 27 – 20 players and seven support staff, as well as all our luggage. Luckily, most of us had experience of how to squeeze in and so we knew the drill. We also had the advantage of our bags travelling in a smaller vehicle behind the bus, so the only challenge was fitting all the bodies in.

Generally, we saw the lighter side of these things and laughed as some of us got comfortable on the floor and others had to make do with a teammate’s lap. But we lost our sense of humour when we realised we had no air-conditioning and the drive was going to last at least another hour. Some grumbling ensued, but we knew better than to complain at such an early stage, and it seemed that things would get better soon.

When we got to the hotel, the building that greeted us looked fairly new from the outside, with freshly painted walls and a manicured garden at the entrance. But when we walked through the doors, it looked as though the hotel was in the process of being renovated, and the outside was clearly the bit that had been made up first. It still looked like a decent place, so we weren’t too worried, and the smell of new paint and the sight of workers installing lights made us feel special as the first group of people staying in this hotel.

All of us were looking forward to being in our rooms and the chance to shower and relax before training. It was only when I saw maintenance workers carrying still-sealed mattresses to the rooms that it occurred to me that we were being put up in a hotel that was not fully ready for guests. I was only half-right. Actually, it was not ready at all.

When we got to our rooms, they were empty: no mattresses on the beds, no lightbulbs in the lamps and, worst of all, not a drop of water in the taps. This made us all a little worried, but we were told it would be sorted out as soon as we had finished our training. We did have lunch at the hotel, although by now I was suspicious of things and particularly of the spread of fish and chicken, and then left for training. At least that went smoothly, and we expected to get back to suitable accommodation. No such luck.

We returned to beds being made but still had no lights or running water. After a training session in extremely warm conditions, we were all dripping with sweat from head to toe and we had to make another plan. A few of our players spotted a river just outside the hotel and said they were going to go there to rinse themselves off. I thought they were joking.

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

When I looked again, the players had stripped down to their tights and sports bras, wrapped themselves in their pristine white hotel towels with their toiletries in hand and were heading out the door. If I wanted to be clean, I realised, I had to join them. My hesitation was twofold: I had never washed in a river before and wasn’t sure whether it was hygienic, but I was also still quite young and didn’t want to expose my body in public. I had to get over my qualms quite quickly. Fortunately, we didn’t have to wash in the river again. No one knows how, but when we opened the taps the following day, the water gushed out.

With that kind of preparation, and Nigeria being as strong a team as they were, it was hardly a surprise that we lost 2-0. We experienced Nigeria’s off the field tactics first-hand. I did have one happy memory from the match, though. The Nigerian centre-back, Onome Ebi, who would go on to become the first African to play in six World Cups between 2003 and 2023, gave me her jersey. We both wore No 5 and she was the first international to give me her shirt. Given how much my Banyana Banyana jersey meant to me, I understood how special and symbolic this moment was, and I have stored it in my memory to this day.

#829. Ronaldo, Maradona, Baggio - what happened to the World XI?

Soren Colding wasn't expecting the call. "The Laudrup brothers, Peter Schmeichel, there might have been some cancellations," he jokes.

Eventually, the Danish FA turned to a Brondby defender who had played a handful of times for the national team.

The assignment? He would be expected to mark Ronaldo and Gabriel Batistuta as part of a Europe XI against the Rest of the World at Marseille's Velodrome.

It was December 1997, and Colding's team-mates would include defenders Fernando Hierro and Alessandro Costacurta, a midfield duo of Zinedine Zidane and Paul Ince, and Patrick Kluivert and Alen Boksic up top.

This was a star-sprinkled cast - one player from each of the competing nations at the following summer's World Cup joining forces before the draw took place.

"Of course, when you see those names, it was just more or less a dream come true," explains the Dane.

Colding was flown to France and chauffeured to the hotel. His driver offered to hang around in case the full-back fancied an impromptu shopping trip. There was no need. Instead, he discovered a bag of Fifa goodies in his room.

"There was the biggest Adidas bag I have ever seen in my life," he smiles. "I found a training suit and went down to lunch.

"Then I saw all the other guys on round tables - they were sitting with their agents, their wives, their family, their friends in normal [clothes]. Then the Danish guy turned in. Nobody knows who he is, in his Adidas training suit!"

Colding struck up a friendship with South Africa defender David Nyathi and the pair were whisked off to a 45-minute training session that afternoon. Not all the big names took part, but one Argentine offered a taste of what was to come.

"Batistuta was there and just to see him and his moves, you thought, 'Okay, it's gonna be a nice evening tomorrow'," remembers Colding, who also got to link up with European boss Franz Beckenbauer.

"He was pretty cool. He was saying, 'what is your position? Defender? OK, can you play left defender?' No problem - I'll play wherever you place me!"

Ronaldo scored twice and assisted three more goals as Rest of the World beat their Europe counterparts 5-2 in Marseille

Come game day, 38,000 fans packed in to see peak Ronaldo. Months earlier, Il Fenomeno completed a world-record move to Inter Milan on the back of 47 goals in 49 games in one sensational season at Barcelona.

The 21-year-old was the most exciting player on the planet.

"It was crazy, actually," recalls Colding, who previously faced the forward when Denmark's under-21s played Brazil in Florianopolis before the 1996 Olympics.

"That was almost the same team as they played with at the World Cup in '98. So we lost 5-1. Just to see his speed and how he played - I played against Roberto Carlos in that game as well - that was just another level. I thought, 'what is going on here?'

"When I saw him there again, it was just to see what is actually reachable for a football player, because that was next level tremendous. His speed and his touch are unbelievable, and also his power.

"And still, just a small, shy guy. You know, he just wants to play football, and all these people are around him protecting him. Just to see when a star like him joins an event like that, how many people around him, agents and followers, how should you navigate all that?"

Ronaldo, captaining Carlos Alberto Parreira's side, was at his blistering best, scoring twice and setting up the other three as Rest of the World won 5-2 - Batistuta also netted twice, before Zidane responded.

"You start thinking what if you injured some of them," explains Colding. "You are a defender, you don't want goals against you, so you have to fight - that's how I am.

"How hard should you go to them? Should you just let them go? No. I would not just let them run and score. I tried to do my best, that was probably not good enough!"

1987: Maradona stars in FA Centenary all-star game

This wasn't the first outing for a World XI, in fact such Fifa exhibition matches had been taking place since England hosted an all-star side in front of a reported 100,000 fans at Wembley in 1963 to celebrate the Football Association's centenary.

They became a semi-regular occurrence as testimonials or charity fixtures, with huge names appearing across eras from Eusebio and Zico to Roberto Baggio.

But the biggest coup was arguably luring Diego Maradona to Wembley a year after winning the World Cup with Argentina and scoring his 'Hand of God' goal against England.

Jon Smith, who represented the Napoli star, explains in his book 'The Deal' how Maradona was offered around Â£250,000 and flown from Naples on a private jet to take part in an anniversary game against the Football League.

"In fairness, he wanted to shake hands with the team and say 'sorry if I offended you'," Smith tells BBC Sport. "He genuinely believed his talent was God-given.

"He was sort of two people. He was lovely, Diego, when you were with him. When he crossed the white line he was Maradona. So the Hand of God was an expression of 'I am God's footballing representative', if you like.

"It was madness, because you can imagine how the media were all over it. It was a bit special."

Napoli and Argentina welcomed the opportunity for Maradona to generate some good PR in England, helped by Bobby Robson's Football League side winning 3-0 - Bryan Robson netting twice and Norman Whiteside grabbing the other.

"I remember introducing him to Bobby Robson," adds Smith. "He put his hand out, and Bobby said 'I'm not shaking that hand!', which I thought was lovely - he did shake the other hand!"

A Ronaldinho XI beat their Shevchenko counterparts 6-3 in February 2005 - Ronaldinho, Samuel Eto'o, Alessandro Del Piero and Gianfranco Zola were all on the scoresheet

One of the final games saw a Ronaldinho XI take on a Shevchenko XI at Nou Camp in February 2005 to raise funds for victims of the 2004 tsunami.

Andriy Shevchenko's stacked squad included Zidane, David Beckham, Alessandro Del Piero, Thierry Henry, Raul, Paolo Maldini and Steven Gerrard.

Ronaldinho could call on Ronaldo, Kaka, Cafu, Adriano, Javier Zanetti, Didier Drogba and Samuel Eto'o, though it was Southampton's Henri Camara who scored twice in a 6-3 win for the Brazilian's team.

But things have moved on, and it is hard to imagine clubs releasing their star players for such an exhibition nowadays.

"The whole world of football has changed," says Smith. "You used to have testimonial games and testimonial years because players got paid okay but by the same token weren't earning Â£100k a week.

"It wouldn't happen now because the business of football is so much bigger, you can't risk the players - if they get injured playing for their country, that annoys everybody.

"But beyond that they are owned by big corporations and in some cases countries, so you just wouldn't allow your player to go out and do that."

Colding went on to play 27 times for Denmark, featuring at the 1998 World Cup and Euro 2000, but retains fond memories of representing the Europe XI.

"Now, to come up with the idea to make a game like this, in combination with the draw, I think everyone will say you are crazy," explains Colding.

"But at that time it was perfectly planned and a fantastic event to be a part of. As players, we have a tremendous relationship between each other.

"It shows all the spectators you can be enemies on the field, but you can actually be friends and gather together in this kind of event.

"That for me sends a signal to all that we are a community in football and we can actually make great things together that not only is a question of money."

In fact, he still has his Europe shirt - a reminder of coming up against Ronaldo and Batistuta and being a team-mate of Zidane almost 30 years ago.

"It doesn't smell very good, actually," laughs Colding. "Sometimes, when I go in the garage with my kids and tell them about it and what actually happened, I see in their eyes, they don't really believe that I was a part of that game.

"That was not about money - we didn't get anything to join - it was just because you represent your country, so it was a great experience, it's also about having fun.

"You know, as small kids, you don't start by saying, 'I want to earn 20 million'. No, you start because it's fun to play football."

Soren Colding still has the shirt he wore for the Europe XI almost 30 years ago

#827. ‘The game is in danger’: PFA head Maheta Molango on Fifa, Infantino and football’s future

At a potentially critical juncture for football, the PFA chief executive talks about the organisation, wider fears in the game and why the Folarin Balogun affair was ‘scandalous’

After five years in charge of the Professional Footballers’ Association, what has Maheta Molango learned? “The game is in danger,” the 43-year-old says. “I’ve learned that the game I loved and led me to first play and then advise and then lead a club and today to lead the PFA, is in danger because it is being forgotten.”

In 2026, with football ubiquitous on all platforms, with a World Cup that generated $15bn (£11.4m) in revenue, and with attendances across the English pyramid growing year on year, it may seem hard to imagine forgetting about the game. But Molango’s unique perspective as head of the English players’ union observes a different picture; one where the future of the sport is being determined not by what will maintain its popularity, but what will make the most money.

“What I’ve seen over the last few years is that I attend meetings where we talk about everything except for the game,” Molango says. “And I think we’ve allowed people to enter the game that did not enter it for the right reasons. They did not enter the game to make it better. They did not enter the game because they loved it. They entered the game because they saw money in the game and because they saw influence in the game. And I’m very concerned about that because, ultimately, if you don’t have a good game, if you don’t have a good product, you don’t have an industry.”

Molango is speaking at a potentially critical juncture for the future of football. Wednesday is the deadline for candidates for the role of Fifa president to put their name forward for March’s election. Gianni Infantino appears likely to win an unprecedented fourth term despite the cascade of scandal that has dogged much of his decade in charge. Infantino’s tenure has also brought about enormous changes of which Molango, whose union had 345 members playing at this year’s World Cup, 27.6% of the total, is highly critical.

The expansion of the World Cup is one central issue; where 32 teams became 48 at the men’s tournament this past summer and perhaps 64 in 2030. The changes, which players’ unions say were made without consulting players, have led to knock-on effects on the calendar that mean the PFA is pursuing Fifa through the European courts to ensure “the legal rights of players to take guaranteed and protected breaks”. But they have also damaged, in Molango’s mind, what should be the sport’s most precious event and for spurious reasons.

“Can anyone who really believes in the concept of the World Cup think that having a 64-team tournament makes sense?” he says. “We may as well call it a summer friendly tournament. And I cannot buy the narrative that says: ‘Oh, it’s about making football truly global.’ That’s just not true. I think it’s disrespectful to think that people in the Congo want to be gifted access to the World Cup. We don’t need favours, we just need opportunities. We want to deserve to be at the World Cup, we don’t need it to be gifted to us, thank you very much. Don’t treat us as if we need to thank you for giving us something.”

Then there is the question of integrity. Last summer’s World Cup brought an incident which, for many in the game, crossed a red line: the overturning of the suspension awarded to the USA’s Folarin Balogun, after an intervention by Donald Trump. “What happened with Balogun is scandalous,” Molango says. “Because my son can say to me: ‘Football is corrupt.’ It’s unacceptable that you’ve allowed a situation where people can think that. Governing bodies must protect the integrity of the game and not just that, the perception of integrity as well.”

Molango was born in Switzerland to a Congolese father and an Italian mother. He is an Italian national and began his career as a professional footballer in Spain, at Atlético Madrid. He made no appearances for the club, however, before moving to Brighton (a club that was a different proposition in 2005: “We were playing at the Withdean and I was washing my own kit at home”). From there he moved across and down the English football pyramid before finishing in Spain. After retirement he retrained in Spain as a lawyer, establishing the country’s first sports law practice, before he became the chief executive of Mallorca. He took the club to the depths of the third tier, then back to La Liga in consecutive seasons before taking charge at the PFA, replacing the longtime leader Gordon Taylor at a time of tumult for the organisation.

To visit the PFA’s smart, new offices in London’s Liverpool Street, bedecked in replica kits and with a timeline of players’ developing rights in the entrance hall, is to see an organisation that has come out the other end of an intensive period of reform. An independent review into the PFA’s governance was launched in 2018 after concerns over the use of funds. The outcome led not only to Molango’s appointment but also to the introduction of a players’ board – now led by the impressive Omar Beckles alongside Ben Davies of Tottenham and Chelsea’s Lucy Bronze among others – as well as non-executive directors and a committee focusing on the ethics of the organisation.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

“The PFA had a credibility issue,” Molango says. “We called an independent expert. They came in, they assessed, and they changed the governance. So I think we led the way. We demonstrated that sometimes you don’t need to be rotten to be wanting to change, you just need to acknowledge that things move on.”

Ten years after the reforms that followed the Sepp Blatter era, Molango believes that Fifa must change again. “It’s a sick system,” he says, “and for me we shouldn’t be talking about individuals, we should be talking about governance. The system as currently constructed is a system that will always foster the wrong behaviour. Because inevitably the decision taken will not be for what’s good for the game. It will be for what’s good for the next election.”

If change doesn’t occur, there is no guarantee in Molango’s mind that football’s status as the world’s favourite sport, and a cultural unifier, will continue. “I think we live in a world where there’s tough competition for entertainment and what I think will happen is that people will lose interest and move on. They move on to other sports, to other sources of entertainment and in the end we’ll kill the industry. We’ll kill it because we’re no longer the only players in the playground. There’s a lot of people and a lot of people who have a good product. I think we need to go back to focusing on the quality of our product. Because football has a real problem.”

#826. Rangers great Brand dies aged 89

Rangers say Ralph Brand will "forever be remembered as a great of the club"

Rangers have paid tribute to Ralph Brand, one of the most prolific goalscorers in the club's history, who has died aged 89.

A Hall of Fame forward at Ibrox, the former Scotland striker, who scored eight times in eight caps, netted 222 goals in 347 appearances for the Govan side.

Brand made his Rangers debut as a 17-year-old in 1954 and remained with the club until 1965.

He was part of four league-winning sides and won three Scottish Cups and four Scottish League Cups during his time at Ibrox.

After spells in England with Manchester City and Sunderland, Brand returned to Scotland to finish his playing career with Raith Rovers and Hamilton Academical.

"Ralph Brand's contribution to Rangers was vast and, through his Hall of Fame recognition, he will forever be remembered as a great of the club," the Ibrox club said in a statement.

#824. Wiegman cites young talent as key to new England deal after calling up Goodwin

Head coach excited by ‘high potential’ of players

Striker Goodwin and keeper Cox in squad for first time

Sarina Wiegman says the potential in England’s emerging young players helped convince her to extend her contract until the end of 2029’s European Championship.

The Lionesses head coach, whose previous deal was due to expire next year, gave first senior call-ups to the striker Isobel Goodwin and goalkeeper Katie Cox on Tuesday as she named her squad for December’s two-leg World Cup qualifying playoff against Ukraine.

Speaking to the media for the first time since she signed her new contract in October, Wiegman described the Football Association as “a trailblazer with the women’s game and a great federation to work for” and said: “I’m really happy with the team but also talents coming through, which is exciting, and there’s now some high potential, and hopefully these talents go from high potential to world-class players, if not already. And I hope to have a part in that, too, and have a contribution to that. While I’m talking about that, I’m getting excited.

“The majority of their development is happening [at their clubs] but when they come to our environment, I hope to have a little part of that contribution.”

The Dutchwoman has led England to three consecutive major tournament finals, lifting two European titles, since taking charge in 2021 on a deal to 2025. Asked whether she had expected that to become an eight-year stay, she said: “No. I thought: ‘Four years, that’s a long time.’ Then it became six years and that looks like it’s becoming eight years. I would never have expected all of the things that we have reached.”

Will she call it a day in 2029? “Well, I tend to think that’s the end point, but you never know! I don’t plan that far ahead. So let’s see where it gets to.”

Goalkeepers: Katie Cox (Nottingham Forest on loan from Chelsea), Hannah Hampton (Chelsea), Khiara Keating (Liverpool)Defenders: Lucy Bronze (Chelsea), Jess Carter (Gotham), Grace Fisk (Liverpool), Taylor Hinds (Arsenal), Maya Le Tissier (Manchester United), Esme Morgan (Washington Spirit), Poppy Pattinson (London City Lionesses), Leah Williamson (Arsenal)Midfielders: Laura Blindkilde Brown (Manchester City), Grace Clinton (Manchester City), Erica Meg Parkinson (North Carolina Courage), Lexi Potter (Chelsea), Georgia Stanway (Arsenal), Ella Toone (Manchester United), Keira Walsh (Chelsea)Forwards: Aggie Beever-Jones (Chelsea), Freya Godfrey (London City Lionesses), Isobel Goodwin (London City Lionesses), Lauren Hemp (Manchester City), Beth Mead (Manchester City), Jess Park (Manchester United), Alessia Russo (Arsenal)

Wiegman, whose latest 25-player squad includes 10 players with fewer than 10 caps, watched from the stands at the Emirates Stadium on Sunday as Goodwin scored for London City Lionesses with a terrific finish against Arsenal. She said of the 23-year-old: “We always knew she’s a huge talent [with] a high potential. We’re watching a lot of games over periods of time, all the time, so we [had] kept an eye on her anyway, but I think it also helped that she had that great goal and a great performance last Sunday.

“She has some different qualities. She’s really fast too. She can head – she showed that also in attacking set plays and defending set plays also – and she can score goals. Does she need to step up to the next level? Absolutely. But you can tell that she’s improving.”

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

Wiegman was unable to call upon several injured players, including Lauren James and Alex Greenwood. She included Manchester United’s Ella Toone, who was initially left out of September’s squad before being recalled for the playoff against Greece. Wiegman said of Toone: “She has impressed us really well. She responded really well. And going back to [her] club, she’s done well too. And that’s what has been fed back to me too.”

Cox is rare in getting an England call-up while playing in the second-tier WSL2. The 20-year-old is on loan at Nottingham Forest from Chelsea.

The Lionesses face Ukraine on neutral territory in Spain in the away leg on 1 December before playing them at Wembley four days later.

#822. Nations League roundup: Devenny’s divine strike lifts Northern Ireland to top tier

Haaland’s late penalty grabs Norway last-eight spot

Parrott penalties help Republic of Ireland secure playoff

A wonder strike from Justin Devenny earned Northern Ireland top spot in Nations League Group B2 and promotion to the top tier of the competition. The Stoke player fired home on the volley from the edge of the area to earn a 1-1 draw away to Hungary, who would have leapfrogged Michael O’Neill’s side in the group with victory.

Northern Ireland had fallen 1-0 behind after a 35th-minute goal from the striker Barnabas Varga, who slotted home when one-on-one with the goalkeeper Pierce Charles after a defensive mix-up. The goal ended Northern Ireland’s proud record of not having conceded in this campaign and also sent Hungary to the top of the group in the live standings.

But moments after Isaac Price had hit the post for O’Neill’s young outfit, Devenny smashed the ball into the top left-hand corner in the 65th minute to restore Northern Ireland’s one-point advantage as group leaders. As time ticked down, Hungary pushed forward in increasing desperation – with Rajmund Toth firing over late on – but Northern Ireland dug in with the defensive resilience which has been the cornerstone of their campaign.

“It’s a great feeling for us,” said O’Neill, who had to watch the game from the stands as he served a touchline ban. “We set out when we came into this level of the competition to first of all try and stay and we knew to be in the top two positions would help us.

“We knew that would help us potentially with the draw for Euro 2028 [qualification] but to come away unbeaten, to finish top, and to give the performance we’ve given against some very good teams, it’s very encouraging.”

In Wales’s group, Norway snatched a quarter-final berth thanks to Erling Haaland’s 96th-minute penalty against Denmark. It was Haaland’s second and completed a remarkable comeback from 2-0 down as the Danes were pipped for second place in Group A4.

Denmark, who began the day in second place in the standings and needed to avoid defeat to reach the knockout phase, led 2-0 inside 14 minutes through Rasmus Højlund and Pierre-Emile Højbjerg.

But Haaland pulled one back before half-time and, after Martin Ødegaard’s 83rd-minute equaliser had set up a grandstand finish, the Manchester City striker scored from the spot in the sixth minute of added time after the video assistant referee had ruled Joachim Andersen had handled in the area.

The two nations finished level on nine points and although Denmark had a better goal difference, Norway progressed on their head-to-head record after also winning the reverse fixture 3-2.

“It’s one of the crazier football years,” Haaland told TV2. “It’s fun to be a part of finishing it off in style. Ståle [Solbakken, Norway’s coach] said ⁠it before the match: ‘Let’s just get a good finish now to a completely indescribable football year.’ It’s fun to be Norwegian.”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Norway’s latest success came ​on the back of their memorable World Cup run, when Haaland ‌and Ødegaard led the country to the ‌quarter-finals in their first appearance at the tournament for 28 years. “It’s completely fantastic and fun,” Haaland said. “I should have had a hat-trick today, ‌but I’m happy with two goals, so that’s totally fine.”

The Republic of Ireland beat 10-man Kosovo 3-0 at the Aviva Stadium to go ahead of the visitors in the standings for Group B3 to secure second place and a spot in the promotion playoffs. The win also propelled the Euro 2028 co-hosts into a coveted pot-two seeding for next month’s qualifying draw for that competition.

Kreshnik Hajrizi’s first-half handball on the line earned the Kosovo defender a red card and allowed Troy Parrott to bury the resulting penalty. The Republic were awarded a second spot-kick early in the second period after a foul by the goalkeeper Arijanet Muric, with Parrott again scoring. Jack Moylan’s header from a Liam Kitching cross made it 3-0.

What had been a largely uneventful encounter took a dramatic twist in the 26th minute, the red card incident sparked by Moylan’s cross, glanced on by Liam Scales to Parrott. His effort – clearly goalbound – was cleared off the line by Hajrizi, who extended his arm like a goalkeeper, and was immediately sent off.

#821. Anne Hathaway Gives Birth, Welcomes Baby No. 3 With Adam Shulman

Anne Hathaway gave birth to her and husband Adam Shulman's third baby together, according to multiple outlets. The couple—who married in 2012—are already parents to sons Jonathan, 10, and Jack, 6.

Anne Hathaway has some news that will thrill you.

The Devil Wears Prada star gave birth to her third child with husband Adam Shulman, according to multiple outlets, with TMZ sharing photos of the actress walking around New York City with the newborn.

While Hathaway or Shulman—already parents to sons Jonathan, 10, and Jack, 6—haven't spoken publicly about welcoming their newest little one, they are more than prepared to take on their new roles as parents of three.

"The thing that to remember about boys is they have feelings," Hathaway—who tied the knot with Shulman in 2012—told Access Hollywood in July. "Sometimes, we think about that more in the realm of girls, but it's just as important to give boys that emotional foundation and make sure they feel just as safe as as we make our girls feel."

The Oscar winner first announced her pregnancy in June, sharing a video set to "Baby, I'm Yours" by Barbara Lewis in which she was seen cradling her growing baby bump in a flowing white dress.

She continued to bare her belly during the press tour for The Odyssey, most notably wearing a red, long-sleeved peplum jumpsuit by Ashlyn New York backwards by mistake.

"I did?" Hathaway quipped in a July 1 TikTok, after man fans pointed out that the one-piece looked different on the model who wore the jumpsuit during the label's Spring/Summer 2026 fashion show. "I did. I did."

But in Hathaway's defense, she's not the first pregnant star to tweak an outfit around her baby belly.

"I've heard from other pregnant women that the maternity hack is if you have to go to an event, you get a dress that has a train," she explained to Access Hollywood later that month, "and then you wear the train backwards and the train accommodates for the bump."

Plus, the Princess Diaries alum considered her baby bump to be the best fashion accessory. As she told E! News at the New York premiere of The Odyssey on July 14, "Cannot be beat."

"This is a lovely microphone,” Hathaway said while cradling her belly on the red carpet, “but I prefer my accessory.”

Besides, her pregnancy was an overall lovely surprise.

"It’s amazing," Hathway shared during a July 14 appearance on Late Night with Seth Meyers, before joking that she and Shulman—who she married in 2012—"knew what we were doing, but we were so shocked it worked."

"We were so shocked it went this way," she continued, "so we’re calling this one our buzzer-beater.”

Read on for more insight into Hathaway's motherhood journey, in her own words.

Anne Hathaway shared the special and exciting news that she and her hubby are having another baby! "It's not for a movie...⁣⁣#2," she wrote on Instagram, showing off her bump. "All kidding aside, for everyone going through infertility and conception hell, please know it was not a straight line to either of my pregnancies. Sending you extra love."

"They get down on the child's level and speak to them eye-to-eye to make their child feel empowered," she told The Sunday Times. "I thought that was really cool. I started doing that with Jonathan."

"I hadn't planned on ever confirming it and then I just, I had seen a photographer while I was on vacation, taking a photo, and I just thought, 'It's such a joyful and a sacred experience, you know, carrying life,'" Hathaway explained to E! News. "And I just thought, 'I don't want the first version of this to be out there with me covering or scowling at someone.'"

She told E! News that getting sleep has been challenging. "Honestly, I haven't slept in eight weeks. I have no idea what I'm saying," the actress jokingly stated. "This is probably going to go down as not the most normal interview on E! News."

"I'm going to stop drinking while my son is in my house just because I don't totally love the way I do it," Hathaway admitted to Ellen DeGeneres on her talk show. "He's getting to an age where he really does need me all the time in the mornings. I did one school run one day where I dropped him off at school, I wasn't driving, but I was hungover, and that was enough for me. I didn't love that one."

"The kind of mother I'll be depends on the kind of children I have," the Ocean's 8 actress shared with Vogue about the ultimate role she has as a mother.

"I can't believe we don't already have it," she shared with Elle magazine, further explaining that "We're encouraged to judge each other, but we should be turning our focus to the people and institutions who should be supporting us and currently aren't."

"I'm not perfect, but if I'm frustrated or distracted, I'm good at making sure he's safe and walking away, calming down and then coming back to him," she explained to The Sunday Times. She said "telling that harsh voice to be quiet" is one hard about motherhood. "I fall short every day, but I'm not going to beat myself up about it, I'm going to learn from it."

"I'm sorry. I am a new mother and I didn't time the feeding schedule—well, like I have any control over it," Hathaway said on Good Morning America with a laugh as she does press for the Alice Through the Looking Glass. "My kid was hungry, I had to feed him, I missed the first 20 minutes so I can't tell you about the beginning of the movie."

"When [my son] Johnny was a week old and I was holding him and I was in the ninth level of ecstasy, I just all of a sudden thought, 'Mommy guilt is invented nonsense,'" she told Elle magazine.

#819. Wayne Rooney says he contemplated taking own life during playing career

Former England footballer opens up on mental health

‘It was probably the lowest point’ at Manchester United

Wayne Rooney has revealed there was a period in his Manchester United career where he contemplated taking his own life. The former England striker said that, even as he flourished on the pitch, he was struggling with his mental health off it, despite being newly married and a dad to his eldest child, Kai.

He said he would spend two days at a time drinking at home and, he told the Life At The Midpoint with Gabby Logan podcast, at his lowest point considered taking his own life.

“I can look back and say I was selfish, but I knew I was going through something which I was really struggling to deal with,” Rooney said. “Then I didn’t want Kai seeing me like that, so that’s why I’d hide away as well.

“I got to a place where you’re contemplating suicide. You just didn’t want to be around anyone. I didn’t want to see people in the streets. I didn’t want to go into shops. I was always comfortable on a football pitch, but everything else [I] really struggled with it.”

In the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.

If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.

If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from the iOS App Store on iPhone or the Google Play store on Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.

Rooney, United’s record goalscorer, said the issues he faced occurred at the height of his career. “You don’t want to show any weakness, so you try to mask it,” he said. “Even though I knew the position I was in, it was difficult to actually admit that I was in that position because I felt like you feel less of a man if you like for doing that.

“I was speaking to a therapist to try and figure out what was up with me because when I look back I was probably at the height of my career, I’ve just had a young son, I’ve just been married. It should be the happiest point in my life and it wasn’t. It was probably the lowest point because of the selfish acts I was taking.”

Rooney, who is currently featuring on the ITV show I’m a Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here!, credits his wife, Coleen, with helping him turn the tide. “Coleen helped me massively. She could have walked away, it was that bad, but she stuck by me and helped me get through it.”

#818. British counterterrorism police arrest US soldier accused of spying on behalf of Russia

A member of the US Army has been arrested near Gloucester in England. Police said he was suspected of espionage activity in connection with Russia. Investigators from the US and UK are involved in the probe.

A 41-year-old member of the US Army was arrested near Gloucester on Tuesday in England, the Metropolitan Police said in a statement.

Authorities searched two locations in the Gloucestershire region, police said, adding: "The country to which the allegations pertain is Russia."

US authorities, the US Military and the FBI were closely involved in the investigation, police said.

The man was in custody at a London police station, authorities said on Tuesday evening as the news emerged.

Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, Senior National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing called it a "significant arrest" as a result of "close collaboration between UK and US authorities."

"The allegations are serious and our investigation is very much ongoing," Evans said.

FBI Director Kash Patel said the case was of "utmost concern" to the US and its allies.

"While this investigation is continuing, I want to send a clear message — this FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners," Patel said. He also expressed thanks to UK investigators across various branches and the US Military Counterintelligence Command "for their outstanding work."

Brigadier General Sean Stinchon, the commanding general of US Army Counterintelligence Command also said the case demonstrated the "resolve of the counterintelligence community."

"The alleged conduct of a senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent," Stinchon said.

The area around Gloucestershire in the west of England, around two hours' drive from London, is home to several sensitive military and intelligence sites as well as outposts for various British and US companies with ties to the defense industry.

RAF Fairford, which was in the news earlier this year amid a security scare at the vast airbase used by both UK and US planes, is not far southeast of Gloucester.

Gloucester's neighboring town, Cheltenham, is one the UK's intelligence hubs outside London. It is home to the headquarters of the country's signals intelligence agency GCHQ.

#816. Fifa’s World Cup TV rights documents indicate hydration breaks will stay in 2030

Controversial breaks were financial boon for broadcasters

Fifa flags possible benefits but says no decision made

Fifa’s tender documents for TV rights for the 2030 World Cup includes a provision for broadcasters to sell adverts during hydration breaks in a strong indication the controversial stoppages will be retained.

A three-minute break midway through each half was introduced for the first time at all 104 matches at last summer’s World Cup in the interests of player welfare, a radical move that also provided a commercial boon for broadcasters, particularly the rights holders in the United States, Fox Sports and Telemundo.

Fifa insists it has yet to decide whether hydration breaks will be used at the 2030 tournament, which will take place largely in Morocco, Spain and Portugal but will also feature three matches in South America, but the Guardian has learned that the possibility and potential commercial benefits are flagged to broadcasters in the tender documents.

The global governing body has awarded World Cup rights to Netflix in Spain and to the public service broadcaster SBS in Australia, and the sales process for the US and Puerto Rico is continuing, with Thursday the deadline to bid.

The tender documents are also understood to reference cooling breaks, a welfare mechanism used by Uefa whereby play is stopped for between 90 seconds and three minutes if the on-field temperature reaches 28C.

Fifa sources told the Guardian the tenders were designed to cover all potential options.

It used cooling breaks on an ad hoc basis before triggering the wholesale adoption of hydration breaks for the 2026 World Cup, despite 31 of the 104 games being played in climate-controlled stadiums, after high temperatures led to stoppages in about 60% of matches at the 2025 Club World Cup in the US.

Fifa said the move was to protect the integrity of the World Cup by ensuring all matches were played in the same conditions, although there were also major commercial benefits for broadcasters.

The Hollywood Reporter reported last summer that hydration breaks were generating between $2m and $9m in advertising revenue a game, leading to claims that Fox brought in an estimated $250m.

Fox’s overall advertising yield from the tournament was $835m according to the media sales analyst Guideline, almost double the $485m rights fee paid to Fifa.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Fifa did not benefit financially last summer but the anticipation of hydration breaks being included could drive up prices for 2030. The US rights are expected to fetch between $1.5bn and $2bn (£1.14bn-£1.52bn) in an auction that will feature bids from Netflix and all of the streaming services alongside traditional broadcasters.

Mandatory hydration breaks will not be used at next year’s Women’s World Cup in Brazil, where temperatures are forecast to be cooler than they were in many cities at last year’s men’s tournament.

#815. Jack Grealish recalls a golden age of mavericks – but football has moved on

Everton forward has magical talent and popularity to burn, but has come up against hard reality of the modern game

Thomas Tuchel has never called up the player he once claimed to love “everything about”. The reason for Jack Grealish’s omission from Tuchel’s first England squad in March 2025 was given as “he simply has no rhythm”.

Catch a falling star? Grealish was suspended by Everton for three matches following “a breach of club discipline”. Suggestions his loan from Manchester City might be cancelled were calmed by David Moyes. Last week, Grealish played in a behind-closed doors friendly against Derby before issuing an Instagram statement: “I want to apologise to the fans and everyone at the club for not being able to help the team the last few weeks.” Amid tabloid tales of karaoke nights and extended socialising, how close is the former boy wonder, now 31, to blowing it?

By many definitions, Grealish’s is an outstanding career. From teenage home town hero with Aston Villa, an emblem of their revival as a Premier League club, to record £100m signing and treble winner with City. All while maintaining a popular public persona, an everyman quality to accompany the looks and the lifestyle.

Even in the Republic of Ireland, the nation he forsook to play for England, Grealish is nothing like the pariah figure Declan Rice is having taken a similar decision. And yet Grealish is fast becoming a tale of charms unfulfilled, talent inelegantly wasted. The trophies he won at City were as a functioning cog, the “rest station” of Pep Guardiola’s machine, not the expressive soloist who won hearts for those rippling leg muscles. At Euro 2020, as Gareth Southgate’s England ground through the gears in the group stage, Wembley crowds bayed for Grealish.

English football is forever seeking its new Paul Gascoigne, the ball-carrying maverick breaking through heavily fortified enemy lines. Garrulous, fun-loving Grealish threw back to memories of football bad boys who made red-top headlines while remaining idols on the terraces.

The tradition was deep-set, from the 1950s heyday of Len Shackleton, the “Clown Prince” of the north-east, to the 1970s when an era of cloggers and roughhouse football was lifted by “The Mavericks” who inspired the late Rob Steen’s 1995 book of the same name. “We treasure them because they embraced risk, because they dared not to give a damn, because, most of all, they dared on our behalf,” wrote Steen.

Peter Osgood, Alan Hudson, Stan Bowles, Frank Worthington, Charlie George and Tony Currie were household names who enjoyed a 1990s revival in the era of Loaded and Fantasy Football League, when football and debauchery were freely coupled. In 2026 there is an entire cottage industry of podcasts and YouTube channels recalling golden days where the pub was as prevalent in a footballer’s life as the training pitch.

In 2026, the elite modern footballer’s is a near-monastic existence. On Sunday, the Brighton head coach, Fabian Hürzeler, described the disciplines Pascal Gross follows to remain a high-functioning Premier League player: “So much work in the shadows, recovery, preparation.” The “refuelling habits”, to use the euphemism Graham Taylor attached to Gascoigne, are not workable for a required body-fat percentage between 8% and 12% or the muscle repair from a target of eight to 10 hours of proper sleep.

Technical ability is the barest minimum. Focused application is a necessity, particularly when player wages continue to climb. Jadon Sancho has winners’ medals in the Europa League, Conference League and played in a Champions League final but, at 26, has not found a club willing to take on a player released at the end of his Manchester United career.

The paradigm player of this age, officially after his Ballon d’Or, is Harry Kane. Both he and Grealish made breakthroughs in the 2014-15 season; Kane as new king of White Hart Lane, Grealish as teenage star of Villa’s run to the FA Cup final. Grealish, spoken of with hushed tones in Birmingham and Irish youth football circles, was the greater talent. Kane’s rise came via a drive to continued improvement from a lower base level.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

As Kane received his individual prize at the London Palladium last month, Thierry Henry, co-compere, made an unscheduled intervention. “Harry Kane is a perfect example that work ethic is a talent, working hard is talent, not only pure skill … this guy had to suffer.” Henry was criticised for comments depicted as elitist, though his point drove at the pair’s diverging paths.

It also recalled the philosophical battle of the 1970s when cavalier players such as Bowles and George, with five and one England cap respectively, were ignored by the roundhead England managers Alf Ramsey and Don Revie. Succeeding George Best, the exemplar of talent unfulfilled, in being British football’s biggest star was Kevin Keegan, whose playing style was all about hard work and energetic running, such that an innate, deep talent was masked.

Best received plenty of second chances. His appearances for Hibernian in the 1979-80 season allowed him to receive a share of Easter Road gate receipts. That same season at Nottingham Forest, Brian Clough tried to get a spin out of both George and Bowles. All three ventures were soon curtailed.

How many chances remain for Grealish? On joining Everton, he appeared renewed. Moyes said after a match-winning performance at Wolves last August: “He probably needs a bit of love and attention.” In December at Bournemouth, Grealish returned the sentiment: “I love David Moyes to pieces.” More behaviour like that he was suspended for and that love will be dashed on the rocks. The maverick tradition Grealish was born to follow and its attendant behaviours belong in football’s past.
